Operations with their maps. BW.4–BW.5 transport completed tensor, evaluation and geometric adjunctions through (B.RQ3). Use B.1e–B.1h for their geometric scope, not BV's opening field hypotheses. Tensor and inverse image were identified above. The common-lower-bound argument identifies the localization map for \(Rf_*\), and ordinary \(j_!\) commutes with localization. Therefore BX.7 gives \[ \Phi_Y\,\overline{Rf_!^c}\simeq Rp_*j_!\Phi_X,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!K,L[m])\simeq\operatorname{Hom}(K,f^!L[m]). \tag{B.RQ8} \] The bar denotes transport through (B.RQ3) and central localization. The second bijection is on the constructible rational categories for every integer \(m\), obtained by localizing B.1h's full adjunction. Compactification refinements, composition, smooth Tate orientation and the closed-support triangle retain their units and counits. Closed exceptional image agrees with BX.2's ambient fibre formula; no unbounded nonconstructible exceptional comparison is asserted.

This supplies the scalar and rational comparison part of B.1d's operation inputs, at that proposition's finite-extension-of-\(\mathbb Q_\ell\) scope. It does not itself construct the ambient enhancements, higher coherence or multiplicative continuous descent also required there. The family biduality deduction remains the separate argument given there; BX.7's field-scope biduality sentence is not silently generalized. The enhanced inputs and strict-heart higher effacement are separate assertions; (B.RQ2) does not imply them.

Mapping complexes and the continuous cochain product

Lemma B.1j (what the existing models supply). The ordinary derived categories used above have actual mapping-complex models. The continuous resolution also has an explicit associative cup product, compatible with the field-topos comparison. We give the maps and their bounds because neither fact alone proves the enhanced exceptional and geometric-descent premises of B.1d.

Unbounded maps. For a Grothendieck abelian category \(\mathcal A\), take the full differential-graded category of K-injective complexes, with \[ \mathscr H^r(I,J)=\prod_a\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal A}(I^a,J^{a+r}), \qquad d f=d_Jf-(-1)^r f d_I. \tag{B.EI1} \] Composition is ordinary composition of homogeneous maps. Expanding the two differentials gives \(d(gf)=(dg)f+(-1)^{|g|}g(df)\); the identity is a degree-zero cycle. BF.1–BF.3 prove existence of K-injective replacements and show that precomposition by a quasi-isomorphism is a quasi-isomorphism on these Hom complexes. Their cone proof works in every shift. Consequently \[ H^r\mathscr H(I,J)=\operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal A)}(I,J[r]). \tag{B.EI2} \] This constructs the mapping model without choosing an additive resolution functor. Products in (B.EI1) are products of groups of maps, not an assertion that products of sheaves are exact. A degree-minus-one map \(h\) with \(dh=f-g\) remains part of a diagram; equality of the classes of \(f,g\) does not specify that homotopy.

For an exact additive left adjoint \(v:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B\) with right adjoint \(u\), BF.4 proves that \(uJ\) is K-injective when \(J\) is. Its component adjunction is the chain isomorphism \[ \mathscr H_{\mathcal B}(vM,J) \simeq\mathscr H_{\mathcal A}(M,uJ). \tag{B.EI3} \] Both differentials are identified by naturality, including the sign on the term involving \(d_M\). Since both targets are K-injective, these are the derived mapping complexes for the two sides, for arbitrary \(M\). The original unit, counit and their triangle identities give these particular adjunction maps. This does not assert that \(v\) preserves K-injectives. Likewise BH.2–BH.4 use simultaneous K-flat and K-injective models: currying is an isomorphism of Hom complexes, with the three differential terms of (BH.13), and the tensor associativity, symmetry and unit maps are the elementary-tensor maps of (BH.8). These are actual chain calculations, not only dimension counts.

There is a precise remaining distinction. BF.6 represents ordinary Hom functors and obtains the triangulated exceptional adjoint. To lift it one must also give the compatible maps on mapping complexes, or an equivalent coherent representing construction, and compare composition and compactification refinements there. Representability on \(H^0\), even with all shifted Hom bijections, is not that construction. The explicit attaching model in Gluing, Appendix B has classical bounded-below field-coefficient scope; it cannot silently replace this arithmetic obligation.

Continuous complexes. Let \(G\) be profinite and \(\Lambda\) a commutative ring, with discrete continuous left \(G\)-modules and \(\Lambda\)-linear action. For a complex \(M\) zero below \(a\), use Galois cohomology, Section 2 term by term. In group degree \(p\) and internal degree \(r\), put \[ C^{p,r}(M)=\operatorname{Maps}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G^p,M^r), \qquad D=\delta+(-1)^p d_M. \tag{B.EI4} \] Here \(\delta\) is its inhomogeneous differential (2.6). For fixed total degree \(n\), only \(0\leq p\leq n-a\) occur. The homogeneous resolution is exact by insertion of the identity; each term is invariants-acyclic by its explicit coinduced-module identification. The same proof works for \(\Lambda\)-modules: continuous functions lift through a surjection by lifting their finitely many values, and coinduction is right adjoint to exact forgetting. Thus the finite-diagonal totalization computes derived invariants for these bounded-below complexes. One may compare with an injective double resolution; the augmented rows are exact and its two filtrations have finitely many entries in each total degree. The resulting comparisons are quasi-isomorphisms. The continuous-function functor is exact, so the same finite-diagonal argument shows that this totalization preserves quasi-isomorphisms between bounded-below complexes. No assertion is made for unrestricted unbounded-below totalizations.

For an equivariant homogeneous internal map \(f:M\to N\) of degree \(s\), its map on group degree \(p\) is \((-1)^{ps}f\). Substitution into (B.EI4) gives \(D C(f)-(-1)^s C(f)D=C(df)\). This retains internal chain homotopies, rather than merely their induced maps on cohomology.

The product and its two gradings. For \(x\in C^{p,r}(M)\), \(y\in C^{q,s}(N)\), define \[ \begin{aligned} (x\smile y)(g_1,\ldots,g_{p+q}) ={}&(-1)^{rq}x(g_1,\ldots,g_p)\\ &\otimes (g_1\cdots g_p)y(g_{p+1},\ldots,g_{p+q}). \end{aligned} \tag{B.EI5} \] The empty product acts as the identity. This is continuous: each function has finite image and factors through finite quotient coordinates, and an open normal subgroup fixing the finitely many values controls the action. It defines a map from the ordinary tensor of the two total cochain complexes to the total cochain complex of the ordinary tensor of the inputs.

Deleting homogeneous coordinates before and after the shared vertex gives \(\delta(x\smile_0 y)=\delta x\smile_0 y+(-1)^p x\smile_0\delta y\) for the unsigned, purely group-degree product. The two terms at that vertex cancel. Applying the internal tensor differential and then the sign \((-1)^{rq}\) gives \[ D(x\smile y)=Dx\smile y+(-1)^{p+r}x\smile Dy. \tag{B.EI6} \] In detail the internal differential on the first factor has sign \((-1)^{p+q+rq}\), which equals \((-1)^p(-1)^{(r+1)q}\); on the second it has sign \((-1)^{p+q+rq+r}\), which equals \((-1)^{p+r}(-1)^q(-1)^{rq}\). These are the two required terms. The group-differential signs agree because changing \(q\) adds \((-1)^r\), while the total Leibniz sign contributes \((-1)^{p+r}\). Associativity follows from the common prefix action and \(rq+(r+s)t=st+r(q+t)\) for a third cochain of group degree \(t\). The constant degree-zero unit is a unit. This product is not claimed to be strictly graded commutative; no higher commutativity structure has been constructed by this calculation.

Which derived product this is. In homogeneous coordinates the same formula takes the front and back blocks sharing one vertex. It is equivariant, preserves the constant-function augmentations, and obeys (B.EI6). The map from invariant cochains to the underlying homogeneous resolution, followed by the inverse of its augmentation, represents the derived counit from trivial-action \(R\Gamma(G,M)\) to \(M\). The front/back product is compatible with this inclusion. Its augmentation compatibility therefore makes its transpose precisely the derived cup product \[ R\Gamma(G,M)\otimes^L_\Lambda R\Gamma(G,N) \longrightarrow R\Gamma(G,M\otimes^L_\Lambda N). \tag{B.EI7} \] For this last comparison use bounded-below input models whose ordinary tensor computes the derived tensor, for example bounded complexes of flat \(\Lambda\)-modules, and resolve the tensor on the source as necessary. The elementary formula alone does not authorize replacing a nonflat ordinary tensor by a derived one. It gives the counit-defined product in this stated model scope. Group restriction and coefficient maps commute with (B.EI5), before taking cohomology; arbitrary nonflat coefficient extension retains its derived comparison obligation.

Galois cohomology, Theorem 1.1 identifies the small étale topos of a field with discrete continuous Galois sets, hence its \(\Lambda\)-module categories. This equivalence is symmetric monoidal: the geometric stalk commutes with tensor because every tensor and balancing relation uses finitely many sections, representable on one pointed refinement; the tensor unit goes to \(\Lambda\). Its inverse equivalence and exactness then identify the derived tensors and the section/invariant counits. Consequently the field-cohomology comparison preserves precisely (B.EI7), in the model scope just proved.

For (B.4) and (E.9) this supplies the continuous-resolution product and its field-level identification, not yet the geometric nearby-cycle descent comparison. One must still compare the actual geometric-generic covering diagram, its pullback to the closed fibre and its products; retain its homotopies through normalized coefficient diagrams and derived limits; and reconcile the enhanced exceptional adjunction above. Complete lattices and their rationalizations are not discrete rational modules. Nor is the two-term generator model of Appendix C automatically a multiplicative model merely because it is quasi-isomorphic to these cochains. The logarithmic change in Appendix E needs its own pairing comparison. These are exact remaining interfaces, not reasons to discard the existing ordinary operations or their proofs. \(\square\)

Resolution graphs and the proper-support mapping bimodule

Proposition B.1k (an actual model before compactification comparisons). The unbounded resolution inputs of BF.1–BF.4 give a dg roof for the right derived functor of an additive functor between Grothendieck abelian categories. Applied to a fixed compactification in B.1e, this gives a dg model of its ordinary proper-support functor. The ordinary right adjoint then quasi-represents the actual right mapping modules of this model. We construct the roof and the representing maps; we do not identify objectwise representation with a completed comparison of all compactification and coefficient diagrams.

Use the cochain Hom convention in (B.EI1). Write \(\mathcal I(\mathcal A)\) for the dg category of all K-injective complexes in \(\mathcal A\). Its degree-zero homotopy category is \(D(\mathcal A)\), by BF.2. Work with the universe convention of BF; if a category of modules on this dg category is formed, place that category in a larger universe. No compact-generation assumption is added to the following graph construction.

Let \(\Phi:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B\) be additive, extended term by term, including on homogeneous maps. Define \(\mathcal G_\Phi\) to have objects \(U=(I,J,q)\), where \(I\in\mathcal I(\mathcal A)\), \(J\in\mathcal I(\mathcal B)\), and \(q:\Phi I\to J\) is a degree-zero closed quasi-isomorphism. A degree-\(n\) map from \(U\) to \(U'=(I',J',q')\) is a triple \[ \begin{aligned} t&=(f,g,h),\\ f&\in\operatorname{Hom}^n(I,I'),\qquad g\in\operatorname{Hom}^n(J,J'),\\ h&\in\operatorname{Hom}^{n-1}(\Phi I,J'). \end{aligned} \tag{B.RG1} \] The third component retains a homotopy, rather than just the statement that the two routes around a square agree in the derived category. Set \[ D(f,g,h)=(df,dg,q'\Phi(f)-gq-dh). \tag{B.RG2} \] For \(s=(f_s,g_s,h_s):U'\to U''\) of degree \(m\), define \[ s\circ t= \bigl(f_sf_t,\ g_sg_t,\ h_s\Phi(f_t)+(-1)^m g_sh_t\bigr). \tag{B.RG3} \] These formulas make a dg category. To check \(D^2=0\), its third component is \(q'\Phi(df)-(dg)q-d(q'\Phi(f)-gq-dh)=0\), since both \(q,q'\) are closed. For the signed Leibniz rule, the third component of \(D(s\circ t)\) is \[ \begin{aligned} &q''\Phi(f_s)\Phi(f_t)-g_sg_tq -(dh_s)\Phi(f_t)\\ &\quad+(-1)^m h_s\Phi(df_t) +(-1)^{m+1}(dg_s)h_t-g_sdh_t. \end{aligned} \tag{B.RG4} \] In \((Ds)\circ t+(-1)^m s\circ(Dt)\), the extra terms are \(-g_sq'\Phi(f_t)+g_sq'\Phi(f_t)\); they cancel and leave exactly (B.RG4). The first two components satisfy the ordinary Hom-complex Leibniz identity. For three maps of degrees \(\ell,m,n\), either association has third component \(h_r\Phi(f_s)\Phi(f_t)+(-1)^\ell g_rh_s\Phi(f_t)+(-1)^{\ell+m}g_rg_sh_t\). Thus composition is associative. The units are \((1_I,1_J,0)\), closed of degree zero.

Why this roof computes the derived functor. Projection \(\pi:U\mapsto I\) is a dg functor, surjective in every degree on each Hom complex. Its kernel, in the order \((g,h)\), has differential \[ (g,h)\longmapsto(dg,-gq-dh). \tag{B.RG5} \] This is \(\operatorname{Cone}(q^*)[-1]\), with the two factors reordered, where \(q^*:\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(J,J')\to\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(\Phi I,J')\). Here the convention is \(\operatorname{Cone}(a)^n=B^n\oplus A^{n+1}\) with differential \((b,a_0)\mapsto(db+a(a_0),-da_0)\). The target \(J'\) is K-injective, and \(q\) is a quasi-isomorphism, so the Hom-cone argument of BF.1 makes \(q^*\) a quasi-isomorphism. The kernel (B.RG5) is therefore acyclic, and \(\pi\) is a quasi-isomorphism on every Hom complex. For every \(I\), BF.1 supplies at least one replacement \(q:\Phi I\to J\). Thus \(\pi\) is also essentially surjective on the degree-zero homotopy categories: it is a dg quasi-equivalence. Projection \(\rho:U\mapsto J\), on maps \(t\mapsto g\), is another dg functor, giving the roof \[ \mathcal I(\mathcal A) \xleftarrow{\ \pi\ }\mathcal G_\Phi \xrightarrow{\ \rho\ }\mathcal I(\mathcal B). \tag{B.RG6} \] In the ordinary derived category, the maps \(q\) identify \(H^0\rho\) with termwise \(\Phi\) on K-injective objects: for a closed triple, \(dh=q'\Phi(f)-gq\) is the needed naturality homotopy. Consequently (B.RG6) realizes precisely \(R\Phi\) of BF.4. No additive choice of \(I\mapsto J\) has been used. All possible replacements are objects of the graph.

The exactness comparison can also be made at the level of these objects. For a closed degree-zero \(t=(f,g,h)\), take \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cone}(t)&= \left(\operatorname{Cone}(f),\operatorname{Cone}(g),q_t\right),\\ q_t&=\begin{pmatrix}q'&h\\0&q\end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} \tag{B.RG7} \] The upper-right chain identity for this matrix is \(d_{J'}h+h\Phi(d_I)=q'\Phi(f)-gq\), exactly the closedness equation. Its diagonal maps are quasi-isomorphisms; the degreewise split cone sequences and their long exact cohomology sequences make \(q_t\) a quasi-isomorphism. Both cones are K-injective by BF.1. Cone inclusion and projection, in both first components and with zero homotopy component, are closed graph maps. Under \(\pi\) they give the usual cone triangle, and under \(\rho\) they give the corresponding target cone triangle. Hence the transferred triangulated structure is respected. For shifts, set \(U[1]=(I[1],J[1],q[1])\); the dg shift on a degree-\(n\) map is \[ t[1]=\bigl((-1)^nf[1],\ (-1)^ng[1],\ (-1)^{n-1}h[1]\bigr). \tag{B.RG8} \] Since shifting both source and target negates the Hom differential before these degree factors are inserted, (B.RG2) gives \(D(t[1])=(Dt)[1]\). Substitution in (B.RG3) also respects composition and the unit. This specifies the signs behind the shift comparison, not only its existence on \(H^0\).

Fixed-compactification proper support. Retain the full scope of B.1e: \(f:X\to Y\) is separated of finite type between Noetherian schemes, and \(\Lambda\) is a commutative ring killed by a positive integer. Choose \(f=pj\) as there. Open extension \(j_!\) on ordinary étale \(\Lambda\)-modules is exact. Apply the graph to \(\Phi=j_!\). Exact inverse image \(p^*\), left adjoint to \(p_*\), makes \(p_*J\) K-injective by BF.4. There is therefore the explicit dg roof \[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal I(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda) &\xleftarrow{\ \pi\ }\mathcal G_{j_!} \xrightarrow{\ F_{p,j}\ }\mathcal I(Y_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda),\\ F_{p,j}(I,J,q)&=p_*J,\qquad F_{p,j}(f,g,h)=p_*g. \end{aligned} \tag{B.RG9} \] Its degree-zero functor is \(Rp_*j_!=Rf_!\): exactness of \(j_!\) permits the K-injective representative on \(X\), and \(J\) is a K-injective replacement of its extension. Additivity of \(p_*\) preserves the displayed cones, shifts and composition. There is no bounded-below assumption, no finite global dimension assumption on \(\Lambda\), and no requirement that its torsion order be invertible on \(Y\) at this ordinary stage. This construction does not yet compare two different compactifications.

The actual representing-module maps. Put \(\mathcal C=\mathcal G_{j_!}\), \(\mathcal D=\mathcal I(Y_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)\), and \(F=F_{p,j}\). For \(L\in\mathcal D\), consider the right dg \(\mathcal C\)-module \[ \begin{aligned} M_L(U)&=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal D}^\bullet(FU,L),\\ u\cdot a&=uF(a),\qquad v\cdot u=vu. \end{aligned} \tag{B.RG10} \] The second formula is the right action for a homogeneous map \(a\) in \(\mathcal C\); the third is covariant postcomposition by a homogeneous map \(v\) in \(\mathcal D\). The Hom Leibniz identity proves both compatibility with differentials and compatibility of the two actions. Thus this is an actual mapping bimodule, before any choice of representing objects.

The ordinary adjoint \(R\) to \(H^0F\) exists and is exact by B.1e and BF.6. Choose \(Q_L\in\mathcal C\) representing \(RL\) under \(H^0\pi\), and choose a closed degree-zero map \(e_L:FQ_L\to L\) representing its counit. This is possible because the target Hom complexes compute ordinary derived morphisms. There is a strict right-module map \[ \begin{aligned} \eta_L:\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}^\bullet(-,Q_L)&\longrightarrow M_L,\\ a&\longmapsto e_LF(a). \end{aligned} \tag{B.RG11} \] Indeed \(de_L=0\) gives \(d(e_LF(a))=e_LF(da)\), and associativity gives \(e_LF(ab)=e_LF(a)F(b)\). In degree \(r\), the cohomology of the source at \(U\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X,\Lambda)}(\pi U,RL[r])\), by the quasi-equivalence and the shift computation. The target cohomology is \(\operatorname{Hom}_{D(Y,\Lambda)}(F U,L[r])\). The induced map is the ordinary adjunction bijection, using the shift-compatible counit. Hence (B.RG11) is an objectwise quasi-isomorphism, for every integer \(r\) and every unbounded object \(U\). This proves right quasi-representability of the particular bimodule (B.RG10), with its maps and homotopies; it is not an argument from abstract dimensions or an unspecified family of shifted bijections.

The remaining comparison is precise. The module \(M_L\) depends dg-functorially on \(L\), but the chosen \(Q_L,e_L\) above have not been supplied with coherent transition maps. To use them as an enhanced exceptional adjunction in the whole diagrams of B.1d, one must carry the representing-module construction through enriched Yoneda, identify its unit and counit compositions, and compare compactification refinements there. Ordinary uniqueness of representing objects is not a proof of those higher comparisons. Geometric nearby descent, the two-term/logarithmic product comparison and normalized adic or rational transport likewise remain separate obligations. The unbounded roof and quasi-representing maps above concern the specified fixed presentation. \(\square\)

The dg-module adjunction for fixed proper support

Proposition B.1l (representing modules, with unit and counit). For the fixed compactification and dg functor \(F=F_{p,j}:\mathcal C\to\mathcal D\) in B.1k, its ordinary adjunction has the following dg-module presentation. There are dg categories of homotopy-representable modules, quasi-equivalent to \(\mathcal C,\mathcal D\); induction gives the left functor on these categories, and a resolution graph gives the right functor as a dg roof. Their mapping complexes have the explicit quasi-isomorphisms below. Their unit and counit come from a strict adjunction on all dg modules, and their triangle homotopies can be exhibited on resolved objects. This is the fixed-model representing-module construction for B.1k. It does not supply compactification-refinement, geometric base-change or coefficient-diagram comparisons.

We give the construction for a unital dg functor between dg categories over a commutative ring \(k\), using the universe convention of B.1k. For its application take \(k=\Lambda\), with the full ordinary unbounded scope of B.1e. Neither the complexes nor the dg Hom modules are required to be bounded or flat over \(k\).

Representables and resolutions. A right dg \(\mathcal C\)-module \(P\) assigns a complex \(P(X)\) to each object and associative unital actions \(P(X)\otimes_k\mathcal C(Y,X)\to P(Y)\), written \(pa\), satisfying \(d(pa)=(dp)a+(-1)^{|p|}p\,da\). A homogeneous module map \(t\) has \(t(pa)=t(p)a\); its differential is \(dt=d_Qt-(-1)^{|t|}td_P\). These formulas define the dg category of modules. For \(h_X=\mathcal C(-,X)\), evaluation at the identity gives an isomorphism of complexes \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{dgMod}(\mathcal C)}^\bullet(h_X,P) &\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }P(X),\\ t&\longmapsto t_X(1_X),\qquad p\longmapsto\bigl(a\longmapsto pa\bigr). \end{aligned} \tag{B.DA1} \] The inverse respects degrees and module actions; evaluating its differential on \(a\) cancels the two terms involving \(da\). Thus (B.DA1) is an enriched Yoneda isomorphism, not just a degree-zero bijection.

Call a module acyclic when every \(P(X)\) is acyclic, and call \(P\) h-projective when its Hom complex to every acyclic module is acyclic. Representables are h-projective by (B.DA1). Every module \(M\) has an h-projective replacement \(P\to M\), as follows. At stage zero take a free module generator at \(X\) in degree \(r\) for each cycle in \(M(X)^r\), mapping that generator to the cycle. A generator at \(X\) means a shifted representable; its action determines its values at every other object. At each later stage include a new generator for every pair \[ \begin{aligned} z&\in P_i(X)^r,\quad dz=0,\\ m&\in M(X)^{r-1},\quad q_i(z)=dm,\\ |e_{z,m}|&=r-1,\qquad de_{z,m}=z,\qquad q_{i+1}(e_{z,m})=m. \end{aligned} \tag{B.DA2} \] Extend by the module Leibniz law. The equations \(dz=0\) and \(q_i(z)=dm\) verify the new differential and chain map. The old module is a graded direct summand; the quotient is a direct sum of shifted representables. Take the increasing union \(P=\bigcup_iP_i\). Initial generators make cohomology surjective at every object. A kernel class has a representative at some finite stage, and (B.DA2) makes it a boundary at the next stage. Consequently \(P\to M\) is an objectwise quasi-isomorphism. This construction involves all degrees at once, not a bounded-below truncation.

Here is also a direct h-projectivity proof, including the infinite union. For a closed degree-zero map \(t:P\to N\) with \(N\) acyclic, build a degree-minus-one module map \(H\) stage by stage so that \(t=dH+Hd\). Once \(H\) is defined on earlier generators, the required value on a new generator \(e\) at \(X\) must satisfy \(dH(e)=t(e)-H(de)\). The right side is a cycle in \(N(X)\): apply \(d\) and use the already established identity on \(de\). Acyclicity supplies \(H(e)\). Extend it freely and keep all old values. The resulting map on the union is well-defined since each element is a finite sum of generator actions. Applying the same argument to every shift of \(N\) proves h-projectivity. In particular, Hom from an h-projective module preserves quasi-isomorphisms, by taking the cone of the target map.

Let \(\mathcal Q(\mathcal C)\) be the full dg category of h-projective modules homotopy equivalent to representables. Yoneda \(X\mapsto h_X\) is a dg quasi-equivalence onto it: (B.DA1) identifies the Hom complexes, and the stipulated homotopy equivalences give essential surjectivity. We will check that the resolved modules actually needed for the right adjoint belong to this category; membership will not be inferred merely from a name.

The strict module adjunction. Restriction \(U=F^*\) is given by \(UN(X)=N(FX)\). Define induction \(T=F_!\) by the balanced tensor \[ \begin{aligned} (TP)(Y) &=\left(\bigoplus_{X\in\mathcal C} P(X)\otimes_k\mathcal D(Y,FX)\right)\big/\mathcal R,\\ (pa)\otimes v&\equiv p\otimes F(a)v. \end{aligned} \tag{B.DA3} \] In the relation, \(a:X'\to X\), \(p\in P(X)\), and \(v:Y\to FX'\); all may be homogeneous. The differential on the direct sum is \(d(p\otimes v)=dp\otimes v+(-1)^{|p|}p\otimes dv\). The module Leibniz rule shows that it preserves the balancing relations. Right composition in \(\mathcal D\) gives the right-module action on \(TP\).

There is an isomorphism of Hom complexes \[ \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathrm{dgMod}(\mathcal D)}(TP,N) \ \simeq\ \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet_{\mathrm{dgMod}(\mathcal C)}(P,UN). \tag{B.DA4} \] From left to right, send \(\psi\) to \(p\mapsto\psi([p\otimes1_{FX}])\); its inverse sends \(s\) to \([p\otimes v]\mapsto s(p)v\). Balancing is exactly the module-linearity condition. For a degree-\(n\) map \(s\), applying the Hom differential to its inverse gives the terms \(d_N(s(p))v-(-1)^n s(dp)v\): the terms containing \(dv\), both with exponent \(n+|p|\), cancel. This is the inverse applied to \(ds\), proving the chain-level assertion.

The unit and counit are the closed degree-zero module maps \[ \begin{aligned} \eta_P:p&\longmapsto[p\otimes1_{FX}],\\ \epsilon_N:[n\otimes v]&\longmapsto nv. \end{aligned} \tag{B.DA5} \] They are natural also with respect to homogeneous maps. For the first triangle, \(T\eta_P\) followed by \(\epsilon_{TP}\) sends \([p\otimes v]\) to itself. For the second, \(U\epsilon_N\) following \(\eta_{UN}\) sends \(n\) to \(n1=n\). Thus these are identities of dg-module maps before taking cohomology.

Restriction preserves acyclic modules and quasi-isomorphisms object by object. By (B.DA4), induction carries h-projective modules to h-projective modules. A quasi-isomorphism between h-projectives is a homotopy equivalence: its cone is h-projective and acyclic, and the identity of that cone is a boundary in its endomorphism complex. Induction therefore preserves such quasi-isomorphisms. This justifies deriving induction with the replacements above; it does not assert that ordinary tensoring preserves every quasi-isomorphism.

The induced module of a representable is again representable, by the actual co-Yoneda maps \[ \begin{aligned} Th_X&\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }h_{FX},& [a\otimes v]&\longmapsto F(a)v,\\ h_{FX}&\longrightarrow Th_X,& w&\longmapsto[1_X\otimes w]. \end{aligned} \tag{B.DA6} \] The balancing relation makes these mutually inverse; the differential and right actions agree. Induction hence restricts to a dg functor \(T:\mathcal Q(\mathcal C)\to\mathcal Q(\mathcal D)\) representing the original \(F\).

The right-adjoint roof and its mapping complexes. B.1k supplies, for each \(L\in\mathcal D\), a quasi-isomorphism from a representable to \(Uh_L=\mathcal D(F(-),L)\). The same assertion, up to homotopy equivalence, holds for \(UQ\) whenever \(Q\in\mathcal Q(\mathcal D)\). Given an h-projective replacement \(q:P\to UQ\), choose such a quasi-isomorphism \(b:h_X\to UQ\). Since Hom from \(h_X\) preserves \(q\), there is a closed map \(a:h_X\to P\) with \(qa\) homotopic to \(b\). Thus \(a\) is a quasi-isomorphism; both its endpoints are h-projective, so it is a homotopy equivalence. This proves \(P\in\mathcal Q(\mathcal C)\).

Define a dg graph \(\mathcal R_F\) whose objects are \((Q,P,q)\) with \(Q\in\mathcal Q(\mathcal D)\), \(P\) h-projective and \(q:P\to UQ\) a quasi-isomorphism. A degree-\(n\) map is \((v,u,h)\), with \(v:Q\to Q'\), \(u:P\to P'\) of degree \(n\) and \(h:P\to UQ'\) of degree \(n-1\). Its differential and composition, for \(|s|=m\), are \[ \begin{aligned} D(v,u,h)&=(dv,du,q'u-U(v)q-dh),\\ s\circ t&=\bigl(v_sv_t,u_su_t,\, h_su_t+(-1)^mU(v_s)h_t\bigr). \end{aligned} \tag{B.DA7} \] Expansion gives \(D^2=0\) and the signed Leibniz identity as in B.1k; associativity follows by expanding the three terms in the third component, and the identity has zero homotopy component. The projection \(\sigma:(Q,P,q)\mapsto Q\) is surjective on each graded Hom group. Its kernel has differential \((u,h)\mapsto(du,q'u-dh)\). After replacing \(h\) by \(-h\), this is the shifted cone of postcomposition \(\operatorname{Hom}(P,P')\to\operatorname{Hom}(P,UQ')\). It is acyclic because \(P\) is h-projective and \(q'\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Replacements exist for every \(UQ\), so \(\sigma\) is a dg quasi-equivalence. The other projection \(\tau:(Q,P,q)\mapsto P\) lands in \(\mathcal Q(\mathcal C)\), by the preceding paragraph. Thus the right functor is presented without a functorial choice of resolutions by \[ \mathcal Q(\mathcal D) \xleftarrow{\ \sigma\ }\mathcal R_F \xrightarrow{\ \tau\ }\mathcal Q(\mathcal C). \tag{B.DA8} \]

For \(A\in\mathcal Q(\mathcal C)\) and \((Q,P,q)\in\mathcal R_F\), its adjunction comparison is the explicit chain of maps \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(A,P) &\xrightarrow{\ q\circ-\ } \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(A,UQ)\\ &\xrightarrow{\ (B.DA4)^{-1}\ } \operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(TA,Q). \end{aligned} \tag{B.DA9} \] The first arrow is a quasi-isomorphism by h-projectivity; the second is an isomorphism. For a graph map, the defect of the corresponding square is the differential of the map obtained by applying (B.DA4) to \(h\). Composing two such homotopies is exactly the third component of (B.DA7). Hence the graph retains the comparison homotopies and their composition, rather than choosing arbitrary isomorphisms in the homotopy category.

Resolved units, counits and the two triangles. For an object \((Q,P,q)\), its counit is the actual closed map \[ \begin{aligned} e_Q&=\epsilon_Q\,T(q):TP\longrightarrow Q.\\ q_{TA}u_A-\eta_A&=dk_A,\qquad u_A:A\longrightarrow P_{TA},\quad |k_A|=-1. \end{aligned} \tag{B.DA10} \] Here \((TA,P_{TA},q_{TA})\) is any graph object over \(TA\). The closed map \(u_A\) and the displayed homotopy \(k_A\) exist because \(\operatorname{Hom}(A,q_{TA})\) is a quasi-isomorphism. This is a concrete lift of the strict unit, not an additive choice of a replacement functor. The first triangle has the specified homotopy \[ e_{TA}\,T(u_A)-1_{TA} =d\bigl(\epsilon_{TA}\,T(k_A)\bigr), \tag{B.DA11} \] by (B.DA10) and the first strict identity in (B.DA5).

For the other triangle, fix \((Q,P,q)\), take a graph object over \(TP\), and lift the closed counit \(e_Q:TP\to Q\) to a closed graph map \((e_Q,r_e,h_e)\). Such a lift exists by the Hom quasi-isomorphism of \(\sigma\); equivalently, lift \(U(e_Q)q_{TP}\) through \(\operatorname{Hom}(P_{TP},q)\). Its homotopy equation and the unit lift give \[ q(r_eu_P-1_P) =d\bigl(h_eu_P+U(e_Q)k_P\bigr). \tag{B.DA12} \] Indeed substitute \(q r_e=U(e_Q)q_{TP}+dh_e\) and \(q_{TP}u_P=\eta_P+dk_P\). The remaining term is zero because \(U(e_Q)\eta_P=q\), by naturality of the strict unit and the second strict identity in (B.DA5). Finally \(\operatorname{Hom}(P,q)\) is a quasi-isomorphism, so (B.DA12) forces the closed map \(r_eu_P-1_P\) to be a boundary. Choosing its degree-minus-one preimage gives the second triangle homotopy. Its existence is justified at the Hom-complex level, not merely asserted from uniqueness of an ordinary adjoint.

All the displayed maps originate in the strict module adjunction, and (B.DA7) keeps their resolution-comparison homotopies in an actual dg category. Different lift choices are handled there, instead of being declared equal as chain maps. Via Yoneda and (B.DA6), this is the promised dg-module presentation for the fixed \(F_{p,j}\). No claim is made that independently chosen lifts for different compactifications, base changes or coefficient extensions already form the required higher comparison diagrams. Those maps, geometric nearby descent and normalized adic/rational transport remain additional geometric hypotheses of B.1d. The ordinary adjoint and its full unbounded scope are retained throughout. \(\square\)

Compactification refinements on the dg models

Proposition B.1m (refinement and adjunction comparisons). Retain the full Noetherian, unbounded ordinary torsion scope of B.1e. For each proper refinement between compactifications of the same map, the B.1k models admit an actual dg quasi-equivalence over the source model, together with a closed natural isomorphism of their proper-image dg functors. These maps respect successive refinements through specified composition identifications. Their induced module adjunctions have explicit compatible units and counits; on the resolved objects of B.1l the comparison is a homotopy equivalence, with the homotopies described below. This constructs the refinement diagram. It does not yet enhance the general geometric composition and base-change grids, nearby-cycle descent or coefficient diagrams.

Write the two compactifications as \(f=p_1j_1=p_2j_2\), and let \(h:\overline X_1\to\overline X_2\) satisfy \(hj_1=j_2\) and \(p_2h=p_1\). Such an \(h\) is proper by the closed-graph argument in Compact supports, Section 3. Its Lemma 3.1 supplies common refinements. Existence here uses the Noetherian-relative native compactification already bound in B.1e; no broader compactification assertion is imported from a citation alone. Put \(\mathcal C_i=\mathcal G_{j_{i,!}}\), \(\mathcal D=\mathcal I(Y_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)\), and \(F_i=F_{p_i,j_i}\).

The actual map before resolutions. Let \(V=h^{-1}(X)\subset\overline X_1\). The induced \(k:X\to V\) is both open and proper, hence clopen, as in Lemma 6.1. Open restriction of ordinary direct image, followed by this clopen identification, gives \[ \begin{aligned} j_2^*h_*j_{1,!}E&\simeq(h|_V)_*k_*E\simeq E,\\ \kappa_h:j_{2,!}E&\longrightarrow h_*j_{1,!}E. \end{aligned} \tag{B.CR1} \] The second map is the open-adjunction transpose of the inverse of the first identification. These are natural maps of additive sheaf functors. Extend them termwise to complexes and to every homogeneous map; \(\kappa_h\) is closed of degree zero. No choice of an additive resolution functor is involved.

If \(q_1:j_{1,!}I\to J_1\) is an object of \(\mathcal C_1\), set \(q_2=(h_*q_1)\kappa_h\). The exact left adjoint \(h^*\) makes \(h_*J_1\) K-injective, by BF.4. We must also check that \(q_2\) is a quasi-isomorphism, rather than assume that \(h_*\) preserves arbitrary quasi-isomorphisms. On \(X\), restriction of \(q_1\) is a quasi-isomorphism from \(k_*I\) to the restriction of \(J_1\). Both are K-injective: clopen pushforward has exact left adjoint, and open restriction has the exact left adjoint given by extension by zero. Hence that restricted map is a homotopy equivalence, preserved by the additive functor \((h|_V)_*\). The restriction of \(q_2\) is therefore a quasi-isomorphism. Off \(X\), unbounded proper base change of Proposition 5.2 identifies the target stalk with the proper image of the zero restriction of \(j_{1,!}I\); both sides vanish there. Stalkwise detection proves the claim. This is the exact derived exchange of Lemma 6.1: on the open its adjoint is the same clopen identification. The common torsion annihilator is retained; there is no bounded-below or invertible-torsion-order restriction added here.

A dg functor, including its homotopy component. For a graph map \(t=(a,b,\tau)\) of degree \(n\), define \[ \begin{aligned} G_h(I,J_1,q_1)&=(I,h_*J_1,(h_*q_1)\kappa_{h,I}),\\ G_h(a,b,\tau)&=(a,h_*b,(h_*\tau)\kappa_{h,I}). \end{aligned} \tag{B.CR2} \] In particular, the homotopy component is not discarded. Naturality and closedness of \(\kappa_h\) give \[ \begin{aligned} &q_2'j_{2,!}a-(h_*b)q_2-d((h_*\tau)\kappa_{h,I})\\ &\qquad=h_*(q_1'j_{1,!}a-bq_1-d\tau)\kappa_{h,I}. \end{aligned} \tag{B.CR3} \] This proves preservation of the differential in the third component; the first two follow from additivity. For composable maps \(s,t\), the third component of their images' composite is \(h_*(\tau_s j_{1,!}a_t+(-1)^{|s|}b_s\tau_t)\kappa_{h,I}\), by naturality once more. This is exactly the image of (B.RG3), including its sign. The units are preserved. Thus \(G_h\) is a dg functor.

The projections satisfy \(\pi_2G_h=\pi_1\). Both projections are quasi-isomorphisms on Hom complexes, by B.1k, so the same is true of \(G_h\). Given an object of \(\mathcal C_2\), choose in \(\mathcal C_1\) a replacement over its source \(I\). Its image under \(G_h\) and the given object become identical under \(H^0\pi_2\); full faithfulness lifts this identity and its inverse to a homotopy equivalence. Hence \(G_h\) is a dg quasi-equivalence, not merely an equivalence asserted on objects.

For refinements \(\overline X_0\xrightarrow{g}\overline X_1\xrightarrow{h}\overline X_2\), use the canonical identification \(h_*g_*\simeq(hg)_*\). At the sheaf level, open adjunction gives \[ \kappa_{hg}=(h_*\kappa_g)\kappa_h, \qquad G_hG_g\simeq G_{hg}. \tag{B.CR4} \] Indeed restrict the two maps in the first identity to the protected open. Both are the inverse of the same clopen pushforward identification; their adjunction determines equality globally. The second identification sends the first component identically, the second by direct-image composition and the homotopy component by the same map. Its graph homotopy component is zero, because the first identity makes its square commute exactly. Direct-image composition on sections is rebracketing successive pullbacks of the same site object. All associations give the same pullback identification; consequently these closed graph isomorphisms satisfy their associativity pentagon and unit identities. This proves coherence for chains of refinements at the actual dg-model level, without choosing an inverse quasi-equivalence for each \(G_h\).

Likewise proper direct-image composition supplies a closed dg-natural isomorphism \[ \beta_h:F_2G_h\xrightarrow{\sim}F_1, \qquad p_{2,*}h_*J_1\xrightarrow{\sim}p_{1,*}J_1. \tag{B.CR5} \] It is natural for all homogeneous graph maps, since those functors use the second component. It respects (B.CR4) by the same associativity of direct image. The resulting roofs therefore recover precisely the ordinary refinement comparison of Theorem 7.1, with its direction fixed by that exchange. No ordinary uniqueness argument is being substituted for (B.CR2)–(B.CR5).

Compare the module adjunctions before making any lifts. Abbreviate \(G=G_h\), \(\beta=\beta_h\), \(S=G_!\), \(T_i=(F_i)_!\), and \(U_i=F_i^*\). All induction functors are the actual balanced tensors of B.1l. For any right dg \(\mathcal D\)-module \(N\), the comparison of restriction modules is the strict isomorphism \[ \chi_N:U_1N\longrightarrow G^*U_2N, \qquad n\longmapsto n\beta_A\quad(n\in N(F_1A)). \tag{B.CR6} \] Its differential and right-action identities follow from \(d\beta=0\) and \(\beta_{A'}F_2G(a)=F_1(a)\beta_A\). For representable \(N=h_L\) this is the map between the actual mapping bimodules, not an isomorphism of their cohomology dimensions.

The comparison on induction is the closed natural isomorphism \[ \begin{aligned} c_P:T_2SP&\longrightarrow T_1P,\\ [[p\otimes a]\otimes v]&\longmapsto[p\otimes\beta_A F_2(a)v],\\ [p\otimes w]&\longmapsto[[p\otimes1_{GA}]\otimes\beta_A^{-1}w]. \end{aligned} \tag{B.CR7} \] Here \(p\in P(A)\), \(a:B\to GA\), and \(v:Y\to F_2B\). The last line is its inverse. The inner balancing relation follows from naturality of \(\beta\), and the outer relation from composition in \(\mathcal D\). For the inverse composite use those two balancing relations to absorb \(a\) and then \(v\). The differential agrees by the tensor Leibniz rule: none of the homogeneous factors is permuted, and \(\beta\) has degree zero. This checks (B.CR7) as a dg-module map with its inverse, not just on representable modules.

Its mate is the closed natural map \[ \begin{aligned} k_N:SU_1N&\longrightarrow U_2N, &[n\otimes a]&\longmapsto n\beta_A F_2(a),\\ \epsilon^2_N T_2(k_N)&=\epsilon^1_N c_{U_1N}. \end{aligned} \tag{B.CR8} \] Balancing is again \(F_1(a')\beta=\beta F_2G(a')\). The second identity is checked on a tensor \([[n\otimes a]\otimes v]\): either side evaluates it to \(n\beta_A F_2(a)v\). For the units one has \[ k_{T_1P}\,S(\eta^1_P) =U_2(c_P)\,\eta^2_{SP}. \tag{B.CR9} \] Both sides send \([p\otimes a]\) to \([p\otimes\beta_A F_2(a)]\). Equations (B.CR8)–(B.CR9) are identities of module maps before taking cohomology. Under successive refinements all these formulas flatten a tensor in its original order and compose the same \(\beta\)'s. Thus their composition and unit comparisons respect (B.CR4); no extra flatness or boundedness hypothesis enters.

Induction \(S\) preserves h-projectives and sends \(h_A\) to \(h_{GA}\), by B.1l. It restricts to a dg quasi-equivalence \(\mathcal Q(\mathcal C_1)\to\mathcal Q(\mathcal C_2)\). On representables, full faithfulness is the Hom quasi-isomorphism of \(G\); homotopy equivalences to representables extend it to all objects of these full subcategories. Essential surjectivity follows from that of \(H^0G\), using Yoneda to carry its homotopy equivalences to module homotopy equivalences. In particular the unit \(\eta^G_P:P\to G^*SP\) is an objectwise quasi-isomorphism for homotopy-representable \(P\): on a representable its values are precisely the Hom maps of \(G\), and the general case follows by a homotopy equivalence. This does not assert that ordinary induction preserves every quasi-isomorphism of arbitrary modules.

Resolved adjoints and their actual homotopies. Let \(N\in\mathcal Q(\mathcal D)\). Choose graph objects \(q_i:P_i\to U_iN\) as in B.1l. Since \(SP_1\) is h-projective, lift \(k_N S(q_1)\) through \(q_2\) to a closed map \(a_N:SP_1\to P_2\), with a degree-minus-one module map \(b_N\) such that \[ \begin{aligned} q_2a_N-k_NS(q_1)&=db_N,\\ e^2_N T_2(a_N)-e^1_N c_{P_1} &=d\bigl(\epsilon^2_N T_2(b_N)\bigr). \end{aligned} \tag{B.CR10} \] Here \(e^i_N=\epsilon^i_NT_i(q_i)\). The first lift exists because \(\operatorname{Hom}(SP_1,q_2)\) is a quasi-isomorphism. The second identity follows by applying \(T_2\), then (B.CR8) and naturality of \(c\); it gives the counit-comparison homotopy explicitly.

The map \(a_N\) is a homotopy equivalence. After restricting along \(G\) and precomposing with \(\eta^G_{P_1}\), the first line of (B.CR10) identifies its composite with \(\chi_Nq_1\), up to the displayed homotopy. The identity \(G^*k_N\,\eta^G_{U_1N}=\chi_N\) is immediate on \(n\), and naturality of the unit gives this assertion. The other three maps \(q_2,\eta^G_{P_1},\chi_Nq_1\) are objectwise quasi-isomorphisms, so \(G^*a_N\) is one. Every object of \(\mathcal C_2\) is homotopy equivalent to a \(GA\); evaluation of any dg module carries such an equivalence to a homotopy equivalence. Hence \(a_N\) is a quasi-isomorphism at every object. Its endpoints are h-projective, so B.1l makes it a homotopy equivalence.

For clarity the unit comparison can also be traced through its homotopies. Put \(N=T_1P\), \(N'=T_2SP\). Choose resolved unit lifts \(u_1:P\to P_1(N)\), \(u_2:SP\to P_2(N')\) with \(q_iu_i-\eta^i=d\ell_i\), and lift \(c_P:N'\to N\) in the second right-resolution graph to \((c_P,r_c,h_c)\). Thus \(q_2(N)r_c-U_2(c_P)q_2(N')=dh_c\). Substituting these equations into (B.CR9) gives \[ \begin{aligned} q_2(N)\bigl(a_N S(u_1)-r_cu_2\bigr)&=dW,\\ W&=b_N S(u_1)+k_N S(\ell_1)\\ &\quad-U_2(c_P)\ell_2-h_cu_2. \end{aligned} \tag{B.CR11} \] All terms of \(W\) have degree minus one and source \(SP\). The Hom quasi-isomorphism \(\operatorname{Hom}(SP,q_2(N))\) now implies that the closed unit-comparison defect itself is a boundary. Taking its degree-minus-one preimage supplies its homotopy. This is a Hom-complex argument with a specified image \(W\), not a claim that the two chosen lifts are equal as chain maps.

There is also a direct check for two successive refinements. With \(S_h,S_g\) denoting their inductions and with the canonical identifications of (B.CR4) and (B.CR7), the composite chosen right comparison has witness \[ \begin{aligned} a_{h,g}&=a_h S_h(a_g),\\ b_{h,g}&=b_h S_h(a_g)+k_h S_h(b_g),\\ q_2a_{h,g}-k_{hg}S_{hg}(q_0)&=db_{h,g}. \end{aligned} \tag{B.CR12} \] Expand the first defining equation (B.CR10) for \(h\), substitute the one for \(g\), and use the strict mate identity \(k_{hg}=k_hS_h(k_g)\); all maps except the witnesses have degree zero. A separately chosen direct lift differs from this composite by a map whose image under \(\operatorname{Hom}(S_{hg}P_0,q_2)\) is a boundary. That Hom map is a quasi-isomorphism, so the difference is itself null-homotopic. These witnesses are retained in the resolution graphs, rather than suppressed by a claim of strictly natural resolution choices.

We have thus connected the earlier ordinary refinement proof to explicit dg functors, their canonical chain-of-refinement identifications, the actual mapping modules and the unit/counit comparison homotopies. The full ordinary statements, alternative compactification input and unbounded scope remain intact. The next required construction is the enhanced version of the general proper-open grids in Theorem 8.1, together with geometric base change, nearby attaching maps and normalized coefficient transport. The present refinement construction does not declare those diagrams complete or certify their recursive foundations. \(\square\)

Proper–open exchange and horizontal resolution homotopies

Proposition B.1n (general squares and the first horizontal correction). In the Noetherian unbounded ordinary torsion scope of B.1e, the proper–open exchange has an actual comparison of dg resolution roofs. Vertically stacked squares give the same comparison as their outer rectangle. For two horizontally adjacent squares we construct the two-stage resolution comparison and its folding homotopy, including the three-input identity and compatibility with exchange. Folding is not asserted to be a strict dg functor. Arbitrary resolution strings, geometric base-change enhancements and coefficient transport remain separate obligations.

Use the cochain and graph signs of B.1k. Let the commutative square be \[ \begin{matrix} U&\xrightarrow{j}&T\\ p'\downarrow&&\downarrow p\\ V&\xrightarrow{i}&S, \end{matrix} \qquad j,i\text{ open},\quad p',p\text{ proper}. \tag{B.PO1} \] The square need not be cartesian. Write \(J=j_!\), \(L=i_!\), \(P=p_*\), and \(P'=p'_*\) for the additive functors on complexes, not for unchosen derived-functor representatives. The right adjoints \(P,P'\) preserve K-injectives by BF.4.

The map before replacement. Put \(T_V=T\times_SV\), with \(w:T_V\hookrightarrow T\), \(a:T_V\to V\), and \(k:U\to T_V\). The graph argument in Compact supports, Lemma 6.1 makes \(k\) clopen. Ordinary open restriction and clopen pushforward give, on every sheaf and then termwise, \[ i^*PJ\simeq a_*k_*\simeq P', \qquad \epsilon:LP'\longrightarrow PJ. \tag{B.PO2} \] Here \(\epsilon\) is the open-adjunction transpose of the inverse identification. It is a closed degree-zero natural transformation for all homogeneous maps. Neither side has been replaced by an asserted functorial injective resolution.

For a K-injective \(I\) on \(U\), choose an object \(x=(I,A,q:JI\to A)\) of \(\mathcal G_J\). The composite \((Pq)\epsilon_I:LP'I\to PA\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Indeed \(w^*q:k_*I\to w^*A\) is a quasi-isomorphism between K-injectives: both \(k_*\) and \(w^*\) have exact left adjoints. By BF.1 it is a homotopy equivalence, and \(a_*\) preserves that homotopy equivalence. This proves the claim after restriction to \(V\). On its closed complement, the unbounded proper-base-change comparison of Proposition 5.2 identifies \(PA\), representing \(Rp_*JI\), with the proper image of a zero restricted complex. The source also vanishes there. Geometric stalks prove the claim. This uses the common torsion annihilator, not an invertibility assumption or a bounded-below truncation.

Define \(\mathcal G_{LP'}\) with objects \((I,B,r:LP'I\to B)\), where the first object is still K-injective on \(U\) and \(B\) is K-injective on \(S\). Use (B.RG1)–(B.RG3) with the dg functor \(LP'\). The proof of B.1k uses only additivity on Hom complexes, existence of replacements and the K-injective Hom comparison, so applies without requiring \(LP'\) to be exact. We obtain \[ \begin{aligned} E:\mathcal G_J&\longrightarrow\mathcal G_{LP'},\\ (I,A,q)&\longmapsto(I,PA,(Pq)\epsilon_I),\\ (u,v,h)&\longmapsto(u,Pv,(Ph)\epsilon_I). \end{aligned} \tag{B.PO3} \] For the third differential component, naturality gives \(r'LP'u-(Pv)r-d((Ph)\epsilon_I) =P(q'Ju-vq-dh)\epsilon_I\). For composition, the third component is \(P(h_sJu_t+(-1)^{|s|}v_sh_t)\epsilon_I\), by the same naturality. Thus \(E\) preserves the differential, signed composition and units, not only closed maps. Its source projection equals that of \(\mathcal G_J\); both projections are quasi-equivalences by the Hom-cone proof. Two-out-of-three on each Hom complex makes \(E\) quasi-fully faithful. Every \(I\) has an object of \(\mathcal G_J\), and full faithfulness of the other projection lifts an identity of source objects to an isomorphism in \(H^0\). Thus \(E\) is essentially surjective there and is a dg quasi-equivalence. Output projection is exactly \(P\rho_J\).

The other roof computes \(i_!Rp'_*\): \(P'I\) already computes the proper direct image and \(L\) is exact. Consequently (B.PO3) compares the two actual roofs for the ordinary exchange of Lemma 6.1. Taking \(P'=\mathrm{id}\) recovers the refinement construction of B.1m. An arbitrary proper square does not make \(P'\) an equivalence; the quasi-equivalence assertion concerns the two graphs over the same source \(I\).

Vertical pasting. Stack a second square below (B.PO1), with bottom open \(M\), proper direct images \(Q,Q'\), and transformation \(\eta:MQ'\to QL\). Under the canonical direct-image composition identifications, open adjunction gives \[ \epsilon_{\mathrm{outer}}=(Q\epsilon)(\eta P'), \qquad (QPq)\epsilon_{\mathrm{outer},I} =Q((Pq)\epsilon_I)\eta_{P'I}. \tag{B.PO4} \] For the first identity, restrict to the bottom open. Both maps are the same clopen-supported direct-image identification; the composition units in the adjunction identify their parentheses. The adjunction then determines the whole map. The second equality follows by functoriality. The same calculation for \(h\) proves equality of the graph homotopy components. This comparison can be performed in graphs over \(I\), restricting the second square along the dg functor \(P'\). Three or more vertical squares give the same ordered product of transformations. The canonical rebracketings satisfy the associator identity because they agree on every section. No choice of quasi-inverse to a graph projection is made.

Why horizontal replacement requires a correction. For two horizontal squares, use the exact additive open functors \(J,K\) above and \(L,M\) below, with proper direct images \(P_0,P_1,P_2\): \[ \begin{matrix} U_0&\xrightarrow{j}&U_1&\xrightarrow{k}&U_2\\ p_0\downarrow&&p_1\downarrow&&p_2\downarrow\\ V_0&\xrightarrow{i}&V_1&\xrightarrow{l}&V_2. \end{matrix} \qquad \epsilon_1:LP_0\to P_1J,\quad \epsilon_2:MP_1\to P_2K. \tag{B.PO5} \] The diagram shows schemes and geometric maps: \(J=j_!\), \(K=k_!\), \(L=i_!\), \(M=l_!\), and \(P_a=p_{a,*}\). Ordinary open adjunction gives \(\epsilon_{02}=(\epsilon_2J)(M\epsilon_1):MLP_0\to P_2KJ\): restrict to \(V_0\) and compare the identical clopen pushforward identifications, exactly as in Lemma 6.1. This is equality of natural transformations on complexes before choosing replacements.

Let \(\mathcal R_{K,J}\) have objects and degree-\(n\) maps \[ \begin{aligned} x&=(I,A,B,q:JI\to A,r:KA\to B),\\ t:x\to x'&=(u,v,z,\alpha,\beta),\\ |u|=|v|=|z|&=n,\qquad \alpha:JI\to A',\quad\beta:KA\to B', \quad |\alpha|=|\beta|=n-1. \end{aligned} \tag{B.PO6} \] All three objects are K-injective and \(q,r\) are closed quasi-isomorphisms. Apply the graph differential and composition separately to \((u,v,\alpha)\) and \((v,z,\beta)\), sharing \(v\). This is a dg category. Forgetting the last stage is degreewise surjective on Hom complexes; its kernel is the acyclic shifted cone for \(r^*\), as in (B.RG5). Every first-stage object has a last-stage replacement. Hence this projection, and then the projection to \(I\), are quasi-equivalences.

Exactness of \(K\) makes \(rKq\) a quasi-isomorphism. Define the object and chain-map parts of folding by \[ \begin{aligned} C(x)&=(I,B,rKq)\in\mathcal G_{KJ},\\ C_1(t)&=(u,z,\theta_t),\qquad \theta_t=r'K\alpha+\beta Kq. \end{aligned} \tag{B.PO7} \] The equality \(DC_1=C_1D\) follows by expanding the third component: the two terms containing \(r'KvKq\) cancel. The first components and units agree as well. Since both source projections are Hom quasi-isomorphisms, \(C_1\) is a quasi-isomorphism on Hom complexes. But it need not preserve composition. If \(|s|=m\), expansion gives the following third component of \(C_1(st)-C_1(s)C_1(t)\), with the other two components zero: \[ (-1)^m(r''Kv_s-z_sr')K\alpha_t -\beta_sK(q'Ju_t-v_tq). \tag{B.PO8} \] Discarding this expression would lose an actual horizontal coherence, even when its class later vanishes.

Here is its specified correction, a map of total degree \(m+n-1\) in \(\mathcal G_{KJ}\): \[ \begin{aligned} H(s,t)&=(0,0,(-1)^{m+1}\beta_sK\alpha_t),\\ C_1(st)-C_1(s)C_1(t) &=DH(s,t)+H(Ds,t)+(-1)^mH(s,Dt). \end{aligned} \tag{B.PO9} \] The minus sign in the third component of (B.RG2) is important. Its contribution to the right side is \((-1)^m(d\beta_s)K\alpha_t-\beta_sK(d\alpha_t)\). The last two terms replace these differentials by \(r''Kv_s-z_sr'\) and \(q'Ju_t-v_tq\), respectively; the unwanted differential terms cancel, leaving (B.PO8). This checks the formula for arbitrary homogeneous inputs, not just cycles. In particular closed degree-zero inputs give the displayed chain homotopy for their composition defect.

For three homogeneous inputs, \(|a|=\ell\), the correction satisfies the exact identity \[ H(as,t)+H(a,s)C_1(t) =H(a,st)+(-1)^\ell C_1(a)H(s,t). \tag{B.PO10} \] To check it, use \(\beta_{as}=\beta_aKv_s+(-1)^\ell z_a\beta_s\) and \(\alpha_{st}=\alpha_sJu_t+(-1)^m v_s\alpha_t\). On either side the third component is the sum \((-1)^{\ell+m+1}\beta_aKv_sK\alpha_t +(-1)^{m+1}z_a\beta_sK\alpha_t +(-1)^{\ell+1}\beta_aK\alpha_sKJu_t\). The first two components are zero. The correction vanishes when either argument is an identity. Products of two correction triples vanish, since both of their first two components are zero. These are explicit normalized composition-homotopy identities for this two-stage fold; they do not assert that independently selected longer folds are already compatible.

The horizontal exchange preserves the correction. The two-square graph transfer sends \[ \begin{aligned} (I,A,B,q,r)\ &\longmapsto (P_0I,P_1A,P_2B,q_L,r_M),\\ q_L&=(P_1q)\epsilon_{1,I},\qquad r_M=(P_2r)\epsilon_{2,A},\\ (u,v,z,\alpha,\beta)&\longmapsto (P_0u,P_1v,P_2z, (P_1\alpha)\epsilon_{1,I}, (P_2\beta)\epsilon_{2,A}). \end{aligned} \tag{B.PO11} \] The output is an object of \(\mathcal R_{M,L}\) by the quasi-isomorphism argument for (B.PO3), applied first to \(I\) and then to \(A\). Both component graph maps are dg maps, so (B.PO11) is a dg functor. Here its source has genuinely changed by \(P_0\); this functor is not asserted to be a quasi-equivalence. Its pulled-back square graphs over the original input are the quasi-equivalences used above.

Folding the bottom object gives \((P_2r)\epsilon_{2,A}M(P_1q)M\epsilon_{1,I} =P_2(rKq)\epsilon_{02,I}\), by naturality of \(\epsilon_2\). For homogeneous maps, naturality with respect to \(\alpha\) and \(q\) similarly identifies both terms of the folded homotopy. Most importantly, for the pure third component of (B.PO9), \[ \begin{aligned} &(-1)^{m+1}(P_2\beta_s)\epsilon_{2,A'} M\bigl((P_1\alpha_t)\epsilon_{1,I}\bigr)\\ &\hspace{1em}= P_2\bigl((-1)^{m+1}\beta_sK\alpha_t\bigr) \epsilon_{02,I}. \end{aligned} \tag{B.PO12} \] Thus the outer-square transfer carries the specified folding correction to the bottom folding correction, with its degree and sign. It also carries (B.PO10) to the same identity below. Vertical transfers respect these equalities by (B.PO4). This provides actual map and homotopy data for the elementary two-square horizontal comparison; ordinary pasting on \(H^0\) alone would not supply (B.PO9) or (B.PO12).

The geometric composition arrays of Theorem 8.1 use the general proper–open square map and the first horizontal resolution comparison above. Arbitrary strings, changes of those arrays, inverse-image/proper-image base change, nearby attaching maps and whole coefficient diagrams require further higher comparisons. The ordinary statements, alternate compactification argument and B.1m refinement maps do not by themselves give the full enhanced six-operation system. □

All-length resolution folding and its higher components

Proposition B.1o (folding without discarding higher maps). Every finite string of exact additive functors between the Grothendieck abelian categories used here admits a strictly unital higher folding map from its iterated resolution graph to the graph for the composite. Its first component is a Hom-complex quasi-isomorphism; its higher components are given by finite path sums. The complete bar identity holds, and every binary parenthesization gives exactly the same bar map after the canonical functor-composition identifications. Proper–open exchange preserves all these components. This is the arbitrary-string folding construction for B.1n. It does not identify that fixed-string construction with completed geometric base-change, compactification-choice or coefficient coherence.

The string model. Let \(J_i:\mathcal A_{i-1}\to\mathcal A_i\), \(1\leq i\leq N\), be exact additive functors. Open extension and inverse image are examples; no assertion is made that they preserve K-injectives. An object of \(\mathcal R(J_N,\ldots,J_1)\) is \[ x=(X_0,\ldots,X_N;q_1,\ldots,q_N), \qquad q_i:J_iX_{i-1}\longrightarrow X_i, \tag{B.RS1} \] where every \(X_i\) is K-injective and every \(q_i\) is a closed degree-zero quasi-isomorphism. For \(t:x\to x'\) of degree \(d\), retain vertex maps \(v_i(t):X_i\to X_i'\) of degree \(d\) and edge homotopies \(h_i(t):J_iX_{i-1}\to X_i'\) of degree \(d-1\). Use the graph formulas separately on each edge, sharing its vertex maps: \[ \begin{aligned} h_i(Dt)&=q_i'J_i v_{i-1}(t)-v_i(t)q_i-dh_i(t),\\ h_i(st)&=h_i(s)J_i v_{i-1}(t) +(-1)^{|s|}v_i(s)h_i(t). \end{aligned} \tag{B.RS2} \] The vertex differential is the Hom differential and vertex composition is ordinary composition. Thus the edgewise checks of B.1k prove the dg axioms for the whole string. Forgetting the last stage is surjective in every degree on Hom complexes; its kernel is the acyclic cone for precomposition by \(q_N\), as in (B.RG5). Every shorter string has a last-stage replacement by BF.1. Induction shows that projection to \(X_0\) is a dg quasi-equivalence. This argument keeps all replacement choices as objects, not as an assumed additive resolution functor.

Put \(\Phi=J_N\cdots J_1\) and \(\Psi_i=J_N\cdots J_{i+1}\), with \(\Psi_N=\mathrm{id}\). Transport every edge to \(\mathcal A_N\): write \(\widetilde q_i=\Psi_iq_i\), \(\widetilde h_i=\Psi_ih_i\), and \(A_i=\Psi_iX_i\); in particular \(A_0=\Phi X_0\). The object part of folding is \[ Q_x=\widetilde q_N\cdots\widetilde q_1: \Phi X_0\longrightarrow X_N, \qquad C(x)=(X_0,X_N,Q_x)\in\mathcal G_\Phi. \tag{B.RS3} \] Exactness of every \(J_i\) makes \(Q_x\) a quasi-isomorphism. The intermediate \(A_i\) need not be K-injective; only the stated \(X_i\) and the final graph targets need be so.

Paths and their degrees. Take composable homogeneous inputs \(t_a:x^{a-1}\to x^a\), \(1\leq a\leq r\), with \(|t_a|=d_a\). For each increasing selection \(1\leq j_1<\cdots<j_r\leq N\), traverse edges from 1 to \(N\). At edge \(j_a\), use \(\widetilde h_{j_a}(t_a)\) and move from level \(a-1\) to level \(a\). At every other edge \(i\), use \(\widetilde q_i^{,a}\), where \(a\) is the number of selected edges already traversed. Compose in traversal order, with later factors on the left. Let \[ W_r(t_r,\ldots,t_1) =\sum_{1\leq j_1<\cdots<j_r\leq N} \operatorname{word}(j_1,\ldots,j_r). \tag{B.RS4} \] Every summand maps \(\Phi X_0^0\) to \(X_N^r\) and has degree \(\sum_a d_a-r\). There are no factor permutations. The sum is zero for \(r>N\). For example, when \(N=3,r=2\), the selection \((1,3)\) is the homogeneous path \[ A_0^0\xrightarrow{\ \widetilde h_1(t_1)\ }A_1^1 \xrightarrow{\ \widetilde q_2^{,1}\ }A_2^1 \xrightarrow{\ \widetilde h_3(t_2)\ }A_3^2. \tag{B.RS5} \] Its arrow degrees are \(d_1-1,0,d_2-1\); this picture specifies one summand, not a claim that the homogeneous arrows are closed. The other two selections are \((1,2)\) and \((2,3)\), giving respectively \(\widetilde q_3^{,2}\widetilde h_2(t_2)\widetilde h_1(t_1)\) and \(\widetilde h_3(t_2)\widetilde h_2(t_1)\widetilde q_1^{,0}\).

Define graph-valued coefficients, of degree \(\sum d_a+1-r\), by \[ \begin{aligned} K_1(t)&=(v_0(t),v_N(t),W_1(t)),\\ K_r(t_r,\ldots,t_1)&=(0,0,W_r(t_r,\ldots,t_1)) \quad(r\geq2). \end{aligned} \tag{B.RS6} \] For \(N=2\), \(K_1\) is (B.PO7), and the correction of (B.PO9) is \(H(s,t)=(-1)^{|s|+1}K_2(s,t)\). The unsigned path coefficients therefore do not erase the earlier sign; it is encoded by the suspension convention that follows.

All signs and the complete identity. Use the larger-universe convention of B.1k and take the bar tensors over \(\mathbf Z\); the same formulas are linear over a common coefficient ring when the functors are linear over it. If \(sV\) denotes the degree-minus-one suspension, write \(|st|=|t|-1\). On the tensor cocategory of suspended Hom complexes, define the degree-one bar coderivation by \[ b_1(st)=-s(Dt),\qquad b_2(su\otimes st)=(-1)^{|u|}s(ut). \tag{B.RS7} \] Extend by the Koszul sign given by the sum of suspended degrees to the left of the operation. Its square is zero: the one-input terms use \(D^2=0\), the two-input terms are the signed Leibniz identity, the three-input terms cancel by associativity, and disjoint odd operations anticommute. These are tensors and finite algebraic identities, not a claim that this bar construction is a flat resolution or computes a derived tensor product.

Let \(F\) be the degree-zero coalgebra map with object part \(C\) and Taylor coefficients \(F_r(st_r\otimes\cdots\otimes st_1)=sK_r(t_r,\ldots,t_1)\). On a finite input word its coalgebra extension is the sum over all ordered partitions into nonempty consecutive blocks. Hence every value is a finite sum; no completion or convergence assumption is present. To make \(bF=Fb\) completely explicit, put \(p_i=\sum_{a=i+1}^r(d_a-1)\) and \(e_k=\sum_{a=k+1}^r d_a+1-(r-k)\). Suppress unchanged arguments in the two sums on the right. The identity is \[ \begin{aligned} &-D K_r(t_r,\ldots,t_1)\\ &\quad+\sum_{k=1}^{r-1}(-1)^{e_k} K_{r-k}(t_r,\ldots,t_{k+1})K_k(t_k,\ldots,t_1)\\ &=\sum_{i=1}^r(-1)^{p_i+1}K_r(\ldots,Dt_i,\ldots)\\ &\quad+\sum_{i=1}^{r-1}(-1)^{p_{i+1}+d_{i+1}} K_{r-1}(\ldots,t_{i+1}t_i,\ldots). \end{aligned} \tag{B.RS8} \] An empty sum is zero. In particular \(r=1\) says that \(K_1\) is a chain map, while \(r=2\) recovers the entire homogeneous-input identity (B.PO9).

Here is a wordwise proof for every \(N,r\). The \(q\)'s are closed and all have degree zero. Differentiating a path word therefore differentiates only a selected \(h_i(t_a)\), with sign \((-1)^{p_a}\) from the selected factors to its left. Substituting (B.RS2) into the first sum on the right of (B.RS8) makes its \(-dh_i(t_a)\) terms exactly these differentiated factors; the minus in the graph differential accounts for the initial \(-DK_r\). The vertex components for \(r=1\) obey the ordinary chain identity.

It remains to check the two vertex terms in \(h_i(Dt_a)=q_i^aJ_iv_{i-1}(t_a)-v_i(t_a)q_i^{a-1}-dh_i(t_a)\). Fix all selected edges other than the one carrying \(t_a\), and sum over its possible positions between its two neighbours. The positive term places \(v\) just before that edge, and the negative term just after it. At adjacent positions these give the same ordered word with opposite signs: all intervening \(q\)'s have degree zero. Thus the interior positions telescope. At a neighbouring selected edge, the two surviving words are precisely the two terms of the composition formula in (B.RS2). Their coefficients are \((-1)^{p_{a+1}+d_{a+1}}\), the bar sign for merging that adjacent pair, including the \((-1)^{d_{a+1}}\) on its second graph-composition term. These are the second sum on the right of (B.RS8).

At the two outside ends, the surviving vertex maps instead multiply the folded output. For \(r=1\) they are \(Q_{x^1}\Phi v_0-v_NQ_{x^0}\) in its graph differential. For \(r\geq2\) they are the two end-split products on the left of (B.RS8), with sign \((-1)^{e_k}\). Every internal split with both block lengths at least two is zero: both graph triples have zero first and second components, so (B.RG3) makes their product zero. These exhaust the differentiated, merged and endpoint words. This proves (B.RS8), including the case \(r>N\), where the displayed path coefficient itself vanishes but the endpoint and merging terms must still cancel. It proves \(bF=Fb\), not only identities on cycles or a fixed finite list of arities.

The unit has all edge homotopies zero. Therefore \(K_1\) preserves it and every higher coefficient with a unit among its inputs vanishes. For the empty string take \(\Phi=\mathrm{id}\), \(Q=1\), \(K_1(v)=(v,v,0)\) and all higher coefficients zero. This specifies the unital higher folding map also at length zero.

Quasi-equivalence and all parenthesizations. The source projections of both the string category and \(\mathcal G_\Phi\) are Hom-complex quasi-isomorphisms, and projection after \(K_1\) is the original vertex projection. Hence \(K_1\) is a quasi-isomorphism on every Hom complex. The \(r=2\) identity makes its induced \(H^0\) map preserve composition. Every K-injective initial object has a resolution string, so full faithfulness of the target projection lifts identities of initial objects to isomorphisms between the corresponding folded and arbitrary target objects. Thus the higher folding map is a quasi-equivalence in the precise sense of Hom quasi-isomorphisms and essential surjectivity on \(H^0\).

We also compare the maps obtained by successive binary folds, not just their object values. Split the edge interval into consecutive left and right intervals. Write \(W_0\) for the product of its \(q\)'s at the specified object level. The binary coalgebra-composition formula gives the higher homotopy component \[ \sum_{k=0}^r W_{r-k}^{\mathrm{right}}(t_r,\ldots,t_{k+1}) W_k^{\mathrm{left}}(t_k,\ldots,t_1). \tag{B.RS9} \] All interval maps are transported to the final category before multiplication. The zero-length right block uses the final object level \(r\); the zero-length left block uses level zero. In a middle split, the right interval starts at level \(k\). These conventions are the endpoint data of the word, not additional choices.

For completeness, the child folds combine into the two-stage graph because they share the middle vertex projection, whose higher components are zero. Its two edge identities are the child identities (B.RS8). Composing with the two-stage fold then gives (B.RS9): the first coefficient supplies the two endpoint terms, and its second coefficient supplies each nonempty two-block split. There are no further coefficients of that binary fold. No extra signs occur in coalgebra composition, since these suspended coalgebra maps have degree zero.

Each selection of \(r\) increasing edges has a unique number \(k\) in the left interval. Conversely, its left and right selections determine the whole selection and the same ordered word. Thus (B.RS9) is exactly \(W_r\). Induction on a binary tree proves \[ F^{\mathcal T}_r=F_r \quad\text{for every binary parenthesization }\mathcal T \text{ and every }r\geq1. \tag{B.RS10} \] The vertex components agree as well. Associativity polygons, including the pentagon, therefore commute as these bar maps: every route gives the same coefficients, not just homologous ones. This statement concerns folds of the fixed resolved string; it does not silently choose resolutions for changing geometric inputs.

Exchange on every higher component. Consider a horizontal string of proper–open squares, with top exact functors \(J_i\), bottom exact functors \(L_i\), proper direct images \(P_i\), and closed natural exchanges \(\epsilon_i:L_iP_{i-1}\to P_iJ_i\). The dg string transfer is the edgewise construction of B.1n: \[ \begin{aligned} X_i&\longmapsto P_iX_i,\\ q_i&\longmapsto(P_iq_i)\epsilon_{i,X_{i-1}},\\ v_i(t)&\longmapsto P_iv_i(t),\qquad h_i(t)\longmapsto(P_ih_i(t))\epsilon_{i,X_{i-1}}. \end{aligned} \tag{B.RS11} \] All output vertices are K-injective, and the output edges are quasi-isomorphisms by the proper–open graph comparison already proved there. Let \(\epsilon_{\mathrm{out}}:L_N\cdots L_1P_0\to P_NJ_N\cdots J_1\) be the ordered composite of the exchanges. Moving each closed degree-zero \(\epsilon_i\) through the next homogeneous factor by naturality, one edge at a time, proves on every selected path, hence on its sum, \[ W_r^{\mathrm{bottom}}(Et_r,\ldots,Et_1) =P_N\bigl(W_r^{\mathrm{top}}(t_r,\ldots,t_1)\bigr) \epsilon_{\mathrm{out},X_0^0}. \tag{B.RS12} \] The same equality for \(r=0\) identifies the folded replacement maps. For \(r=1\) the endpoint vertex maps are also those of the outer graph transfer. For \(r\geq2\) both endpoint components are zero. Thus exchange commutes with every Taylor coefficient of folding and with (B.RS10). There is no degree sign hidden in moving an exchange: its degree is zero. The vertical pasting identity (B.PO4) makes successive vertical transfers give this same comparison for the outer vertical rectangle. This closes the arbitrary-length horizontal-folding comparison for these proper–open strings, while preserving all specified homotopies.

The exactness and K-injective arguments apply to unbounded complexes; no finite global dimension, coefficient flatness or bounded-below condition has been inserted. The path sums are finite because a composition string has finitely many edges, not because the complexes are bounded. What remains is to construct the actual inverse-image/proper-image base-change graph comparisons and integrate changing compactification arrays, then the geometric nearby attaching maps and whole normalized coefficient diagrams. □

Canonical proper base change on resolution graphs

Proposition B.1p (the enhanced comparison for proper squares). Let \(\Lambda\) be a commutative ring with \(n\Lambda=0\) for some positive integer \(n\). In a cartesian square of schemes \[ \begin{matrix} X'&\xrightarrow{a}&X\\ f'\downarrow&&\downarrow f\\ Y'&\xrightarrow{g}&Y, \end{matrix} \qquad f\text{ proper}, \tag{B.BC1} \] use the small étale sites and inverse images of sheaves of \(\Lambda\)-modules. The canonical proper-base-change map has the dg graph presentation below for all unbounded complexes. It respects vertical composition of proper maps and every higher folding component for every finite sequence of base changes. These are comparisons of specified models; the further integration with changing compactifications, exceptional adjunctions and nearby-cycle pairings is not inferred from them.

There is no Noetherian, bounded-below, finite-global-dimension or invertibility-of-\(n\) assumption in this proper-square assertion. The common annihilator is essential to the invoked unbounded provider. Proper base change, §1 separately supplies the bounded-below torsion-cohomology theorem over arbitrary coefficients; that does not supply an unrestricted unbounded arbitrary-ring extension.

Keep the canonical map. Write \(A=a^*\), \(G=g^*\), \(P=f_*\), and \(P'=f'_*\). The inverse-image functors are exact. Direct image preserves K-injectives by the actual Hom-complex adjunction of BF.4. Let \(\eta^a\) be the unit of \(a^*\dashv a_*\), and \(\epsilon^g\) the counit of \(g^*\dashv g_*\). Using \(Pa_*\cong g_*P'\), the underived comparison, extended termwise, is the closed degree-zero natural transformation \[ \begin{aligned} \beta&:GP\longrightarrow P'A,\\ \beta_M&=\epsilon^g_{P'AM}\,G(P\eta^a_M),\\ (P'A u)\beta_I&=\beta_{I'}(GPu). \end{aligned} \tag{B.BC2} \] for every homogeneous \(u:I\to I'\), not just chain maps. Indeed the sheaf naturality identity holds on each component \(u^k:I^k\to I'^{k+|u|}\); the transformation is of degree zero, so no sign is introduced. Commutation with the complex differential follows by applying the same identity to \(d_I\).

Take \(I\) K-injective on \(X\), and any closed quasi-isomorphism \(q:AI\to J\) with \(J\) K-injective on \(X'\). The map \[ \alpha_{I,J,q}=(P'q)\beta_I: GPI\longrightarrow P'J \tag{B.BC3} \] is a quasi-isomorphism. Here is why it is the required map rather than an abstract isomorphism. The source computes \(g^*Rf_*I\), since \(I\) is K-injective and \(G\) is exact. The target computes \(Rf'_*a^*I\). The adjunction construction in §1 of the proper-base-change lesson identifies (B.BC3) with its canonical comparison. Compact support, Proposition 5.2 proves that this very map is invertible: locally a finite fibre-dimension bound gives finite cohomological amplitude; for a termwise injective K-injective resolution the pulled-back terms are \(f'_*\)-acyclic, and Lemma 5.1 permits their unbounded complex to compute the derived image. No exactness of \(P'\) on arbitrary complexes is asserted. To pass to an arbitrary K-injective representative, compare it by a quasi-isomorphism with a termwise injective K-injective representative, using BF.1. That map is a homotopy equivalence, preserved by all the termwise additive functors here. Lift the corresponding map between the chosen pulled-back replacements by the BF.1 Hom quasi-isomorphism. Its naturality homotopy survives \(P'\). Hence the canonical map for the arbitrary representative is the same derived isomorphism.

The two graphs share the original input. Form \(\mathcal G_A\) and \(\mathcal G_{GP}\) over \(\mathcal I(X_{\mathrm{et}},\Lambda)\), with their respective target K-injective categories on \(X'\) and \(Y'\). The functor \(GP\) is additive but need not be exact. This is allowed: the proof of (B.RG5) uses only a K-injective graph target and the quasi-isomorphism of its replacement. Every complex \(GPI\) has such a replacement. Define \[ \begin{aligned} E_{f,g}(I,J,q)&=(I,P'J,(P'q)\beta_I),\\ E_{f,g}(u,v,h)&=(u,P'v,(P'h)\beta_I). \end{aligned} \tag{B.BC4} \] The first entry is \(I\), not \(PI\). In a degree-\(d\) triple, \(h:AI\to J'\) has degree \(d-1\), so its image has source \(GPI\), target \(P'J'\), and that same degree. Equation (B.BC3) and preservation of K-injectives make the object formula valid.

The third component of the target differential is \[ \begin{aligned} &(P'q')\beta_{I'}GPu-(P'v)(P'q)\beta_I -d((P'h)\beta_I)\\ &\hspace{1em}=P'(q'Au-vq-dh)\beta_I. \end{aligned} \tag{B.BC5} \] For \(|s|=m\), its composition component is \(P'(h_sAu_t+(-1)^m v_sh_t)\beta_I\), by (B.BC2). Thus (B.BC4) is a unital dg functor. Both graph projections to the same \(I\) are quasi-equivalences by (B.RG5), and \(\pi E_{f,g}=\pi\). It follows on Hom complexes by two-out-of-three that \(E_{f,g}\) is a quasi-isomorphism. For essential surjectivity, choose an \(A\)-replacement over the original input of a target graph object. Full faithfulness of the target projection on \(H^0\) lifts the identity of that input to an isomorphism between the two target graph objects. This proves that \(E_{f,g}\) is a dg quasi-equivalence. It does not claim that \(P\), or a functor changing the source to \(PI\), is an equivalence.

The target projection after (B.BC4) is exactly \(P'\rho_A\). Together with the quasi-equivalences on the left, it compares the roof for \(g^*Rf_*\) with the roof for \(Rf'_*a^*\). Closed degree-zero triples retain the naturality homotopy in (B.BC5); higher homogeneous triples are not discarded.

Vertical proper composites. Stack a cartesian proper square for \(p:Y\to Z\), with inverse image \(H=h^*\), direct images \(R=p_*\), \(R'=p'_*\), and comparison \(\gamma:HR\to R'G\). The adjunction units give, under the canonical direct-image composition identifications, \[ \beta_{pf,h}=(R'\beta)(\gamma P): HRP\longrightarrow R'P'A. \tag{B.BC6} \] This is an equality of termwise natural transformations. Substitute the unit/counit formula (B.BC2) for the two factors on the right and transpose through \(H\dashv h_*\). Naturality moves the unit for \(a\) past the middle comparison; the unit and counit of \(G\dashv g_*\) then cancel by the triangle identity. The remaining transpose is \(RP\eta^a\), followed by \(RPa_*\cong h_*R'P'\), exactly the transpose of the left side. This also specifies the direct-image composition convention in §1 of the proper-base-change provider.

Do not compose wrongly typed graph functors. First (B.BC4) gives an edge \(G(PI)\to P'J\); its input on \(Y\) is the K-injective \(PI\). Apply the second square to that edge, retaining the original label \(I\) and forcing its input maps to be \(Pu\). The resulting graph over \(I\) has object map and homotopy component \[ \begin{aligned} &(R'P'q)(R'\beta_I)\gamma_{PI},\\ &(R'P'h)(R'\beta_I)\gamma_{PI}, \end{aligned} \tag{B.BC7} \] and vertices \((I,R'P'J)\), with maps \((u,R'P'v)\). By (B.BC6) these are exactly the direct outer-square formulas. For three or more vertical proper maps, iterating the composite-unit formula and ordinary associativity gives the same ordered factors; this proves all finite vertical pasting identities, including identities. The canonical composition identifications are retained, not replaced by literal equality of differently bracketed sheaf functors.

Successive base changes and every higher component. Let \(Y_N\to\cdots\to Y_0\) be any finite string of base maps, let \(X_i=X_0\times_{Y_0}Y_i\), and let \(f_i:X_i\to Y_i\) be the pulled-back proper maps. Put \(A_i=a_i^*\), \(G_i=g_i^*\), \(P_i=f_{i,*}\). Each square has \(\beta_i:G_iP_{i-1}\to P_iA_i\). For an \(A\)-resolution string \((I_i,q_i)\) of B.1o, set \[ \begin{aligned} I_i^{Y}&=P_iI_i,& q_i^{Y}&=(P_iq_i)\beta_{i,I_{i-1}},\\ v_i^{Y}(t)&=P_iv_i(t),& h_i^{Y}(t)&=(P_ih_i(t))\beta_{i,I_{i-1}}. \end{aligned} \tag{B.BC8} \] Every vertex is K-injective and every replacement is a quasi-isomorphism by (B.BC3), applied to the K-injective \(I_{i-1}\). The differential and composition calculation (B.BC5) works on each edge. To compare equivalent source models, define the pulled-back \(G\)-string category to retain \(I_0\), with first vertex forced to be \(P_0I_0\) and its map forced to be \(P_0u\). All later vertices and edges remain free replacement data. Its projection to \(I_0\) is a quasi-equivalence: forget the final stage successively, using the same acyclic Hom cones as (B.RG5); the length-zero category is precisely \(\mathcal I(X_0)\).
