Naturality of the signed evaluations, together with the block witness, gives a whole map \(A_e^{\mathrm f}:K_i\to DW_j[-1]\) satisfying \[ E_jB_e-(D\lambda_e^{\mathrm f})E_i=dA_e^{\mathrm f}. \tag{B.FK5} \] This is naturality of the explicit B.FK3 map. For a homotopy in a right tensor factor the action on a homogeneous tensor is \((1\otimes h)(x\otimes y)=(-1)^{|x|}x\otimes h(y)\). Tensoring the block equation with this convention and applying the degree-zero evaluation therefore proves B.FK5, including its sign. The associator compatibility B.RK4 gives the same result for either parenthesization.

Keep the originally specified \(\lambda_e,\omega_e\) of B.MX5. The factorized edge has its own \(\omega_e^{\mathrm f}\), formed by whiskering the original block witness and composing with the remaining factors and the sheaf map \(\tau_i\) of B.MX3. The equality of the raw geometric composites gives \[ a_i\lambda_e^{\mathrm f}-a_j=d\omega_e^{\mathrm f}, \qquad a_i\lambda_e-a_j=d\omega_e. \tag{B.FK6} \] If the two lifts differ, B.ND7 applied to \(\operatorname{Hom}(W_j,a_i)\) supplies the full comparison \[ \begin{aligned} dh_e&=\lambda_e^{\mathrm f}-\lambda_e,\\ a_i h_e-(\omega_e^{\mathrm f}-\omega_e)&=dq_e, \qquad |h_e|=-1,\quad |q_e|=-2. \end{aligned} \tag{B.FK7} \] For existence, the first difference becomes a boundary under this Hom quasi-isomorphism. Lift its primitive, then correct it by a closed degree-minus-one map so that the second difference is a boundary, exactly as in B.WI8–9. This keeps both original witnesses. If the two choices coincide, take \(h_e=q_e=0\).

Set \[ A_e=A_e^{\mathrm f}+(Dh_e)E_i. \tag{B.FK8} \] Since \(d(Dh_e)=D(dh_e)\), equations B.FK5 and B.FK7 give \[ E_jB_e-(D\lambda_e)E_i=dA_e. \tag{B.FK9} \] The higher map \(q_e\) is retained in the full comparison of the two left resolution-graph edges. In the ordinary arrow-graph convention that comparison is \((h_e,0,q_e)\). Its signed dual is \((0,Dh_e,-Dq_e)\), by B.RD2. Thus B.FK8 is its map component after evaluation; it does not discard the third coordinate \(-Dq_e\). The factorized right edge has now been attached to the fixed original left edge, rather than silently replacing that edge or its mixed cell.

3. Transfer the actual mixed generator

Let \(p:R\to\mathcal W\) be B.MP7 and put \(N=DR\), as in B.WI1. Define \[ \widetilde E_i=(Dp_i)E_i, \qquad \widetilde A_e=(Dp_j)A_e. \tag{B.FK10} \] Each \(Dp_i\) is a homotopy equivalence by B.RD6. The maps \(\widetilde E_i:K_i\to N_i\) are therefore whole quasi-isomorphisms. Strict naturality of \(p\), with the signed dual convention, gives \[ \widetilde E_jB_e-N(e)\widetilde E_i=d\widetilde A_e. \tag{B.FK11} \] The common target is the actual diagram \(N\), with \(n=N(c^\vee)\), and not an unspecified equivalent diagram.

Write \[ T_K=B_{23}B_{12}B_{01}, \qquad B_K=B_{53}B_{45}B_{04}, \qquad \Delta_K=T_K-B_K. \tag{B.FK12} \] The two path witnesses in the target are \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega_T={}&\widetilde A_{23}B_{12}B_{01} +N(e_{23})\widetilde A_{12}B_{01} +N(e_{23})N(e_{12})\widetilde A_{01},\\ \Omega_B={}&\widetilde A_{53}B_{45}B_{04} +N(e_{53})\widetilde A_{45}B_{04} +N(e_{53})N(e_{45})\widetilde A_{04}. \end{aligned} \tag{B.FK13} \] Here edge symbols in \(N\) have the right orientation of \(\mathcal I\); equivalently they are the opposite edges of B.MP1. Telescoping B.FK11 gives \[ d(\Omega_T-\Omega_B) =\widetilde E_3\Delta_K -\bigl(N(T^\vee)-N(B^\vee)\bigr)\widetilde E_0. \tag{B.FK14} \] The degree-minus-one map \[ \Xi=n\widetilde E_0+\Omega_T-\Omega_B \tag{B.FK15} \] therefore satisfies \(d\Xi=\widetilde E_3\Delta_K\). The cancellation uses \(dn=N(T^\vee)-N(B^\vee)\), including both paths. Since \(K_0\) is whole h-projective, B.ND7 supplies maps \[ \begin{aligned} dH_K&=\Delta_K,\\ \widetilde E_3H_K-\Xi&=dQ_K,\\ |H_K|&=-1,\qquad |Q_K|=-2. \end{aligned} \tag{B.FK16} \] Use the same two-stage primitive-and-closed-correction argument as B.WI9. This proves both equations with the specified \(\Xi\). Choosing an arbitrary primitive of \(\Delta_K\) would not suffice.

To see the full diagram, a homogeneous arrow between \((K_i,N_i,\widetilde E_i)\) and \((K_j,N_j,\widetilde E_j)\) is a triple \((b,f,h)\), with \[ \begin{aligned} D(b,f,h)&=(db,df,\widetilde E_j b-f\widetilde E_i-dh),\\ (b',f',h')(b,f,h)&=(b'b,f'f,h'b+(-1)^{|f'|}f'h). \end{aligned} \tag{B.FK17} \] These are the ordinary signed graph formulas, with the source component listed first. Assign an edge the triple \((B_e,N(e),\widetilde A_e)\), and assign the free mixed generator the triple \((H_K,n,Q_K)\). Equations B.FK12–16 say exactly that its differential is the top graph path minus the bottom graph path. Freeness then gives a strict dg diagram on all of \(\mathcal I\). The third component carries the full target witness; projection to the source diagram alone would lose it.

4. Whole resolutions and the homogeneous inverse comparison

The source diagram just constructed has the actual factored kernels \(K_i\) as vertices and the factored elementary maps \(B_e\) as edges. Its values are h-projective, but whole-index h-projectivity is a separate assertion. Apply the signed parameter-bar construction B.KC9–10 to its graph comparison with \(N\). The object maps are \(\widetilde E_i\), the edge homotopies are \(\widetilde A_e\), and the value on \(c^\vee\) is \(Q_K\). B.FK17 is precisely the differential and composition condition for this construction. It produces a strict whole-diagram quasi-isomorphism \[ \Psi_K:B(\mathcal I(-,-),\mathcal I,K)\longrightarrow N. \tag{B.FK18} \] At the distinguished length-one tensor its value is \[ \Psi_{K,3}(1_3\otimes c^\vee\otimes x)=-Q_Kx. \tag{B.FK19} \] The sign and degree follow from B.KC10: the identity has degree zero, and a length-one tensor with \(|c^\vee|=-1\) has total degree \(|x|-2\). The quasi-isomorphism follows from the representable-bar contraction and the quasi-isomorphisms \(\widetilde E_i\); no inverse of the unresolved raw target is used.

Resolve this whole bar diagram by B.ND5 before choosing whole inverses. It has its ordinary augmentation to the factored diagram \(K\), and its map B.FK18 to the specific \(N\). Thus it supplies a whole resolution roof of \(N\) connected by actual maps to all six factored right-kernel words. The original KC factor roofs, their inverse-cancellation homotopies, the comparison pairs B.FK7 and their signed duals, and B.RD8's raw-target witness remain in the diagram. A given nested UQ face retains its original \(K_2\) coefficient under these strict bar maps as in B.MX12; this statement does not add an unspecified higher face.

Two such constructions over this same mixed index give admissible roofs for B.WI3–16. Its inverse comparison can consequently be made on whole resolutions of the factored six-vertex diagrams. B.WI17–18 still governs comparison with prescribed endpoint homotopies. For evaluation on an h-projective source module, a degree-\(r\) kernel map acts by \(x\otimes z\mapsto(-1)^{r|x|}x\otimes f(z)\); the tensor differential proves that this preserves B.FK16 and every graph boundary. The result therefore concerns actual functors on resolved inputs and their homogeneous maps.

The fixed proper–open/base-change mixed diagram and its six geometric right-word factorizations are linked by these explicit evaluation roofs and full comparison witnesses. The direct-versus-ordered maps \(s:S_d\to S_o\) and \(v:V_d\to V_o\) for two successive changes of base additionally involve their compositor diagram B.OD11–19. Identifying that combined parameter diagram with these fixed mixed diagrams, and comparing its chosen inverse homotopies, are separate requirements; two copies of B.FK18 alone do not identify those differently indexed functors. The common-index transport needed for B.RCmp1, its higher triangle comparisons, changing-array coherence, nearby-cycle descent and normalized coefficient completion retain those obligations. \(\square\)

Join the direct and ordered mixed diagrams over their geometric target

Proposition B.1bi (the compositor prism). For two successive cartesian base changes of the proper–open square, the direct and ordered six-vertex left-kernel diagrams admit a common free parameter diagram. Its vertex comparisons are the actual inverse-image compositors. It retains both original mixed cells and all six edge witnesses. The comparison between the mixed cells has degree minus two and a degree-minus-three witness in the common geometric mapping complex. Whole resolution and signed duality give the corresponding right-kernel parameter diagram, with the direct-to-ordered orientation of the inverse-image maps.

Use the Noetherian separated finite-type geometry and ordinary unbounded torsion coefficients of B.MX, including the proper-base-change annihilator hypothesis. The module arguments use the original commutative coefficient ring. Write the three cartesian rows as \[ \begin{array}{ccc} U_r&\xrightarrow{h_r}&Y_r\\ {\scriptstyle k_r}\downarrow&&\downarrow{\scriptstyle i_r}\\ C_r&\xrightarrow{p_r}&D_r \qquad r=0,1,2, \end{array} \] where \(h_r,p_r\) are proper and \(i_r,k_r\) are open. The vertical maps are \(a_{T,1}:T_1\to T_0\), \(a_{T,2}:T_2\to T_1\), and \(a_{T,21}=a_{T,1}a_{T,2}\), for \(T=U,Y,C,D\). Let \(A_{T,r}=a_{T,r}^*\). The inverse-image compositor identifies \(A_{T,21}\) with \(A_{T,2}A_{T,1}\); keep that actual natural isomorphism whenever the two expressions meet.

1. The twelve words and their common augmentation

In the following table \(\mathbb L_F\) denotes the left kernel of an elementary operation. Put \[ \begin{gathered} Z_T^d=\mathbb L_{A_{T,21}},\qquad Z_T^o=\mathbb L_{A_{T,2}}\mathbb L_{A_{T,1}},\\ c_T:Z_T^o\longrightarrow Z_T^d. \end{gathered}\tag{B.PR1} \] The map \(c_T\) is B.OD3's whole lift of the inverse-image compositor, with its augmentation homotopy. Products are in left-kernel order. For \(\sigma=d,o\), set \[ \begin{array}{c|l|l} v&W_v^\sigma&C_v:W_v^o\longrightarrow W_v^d\\ \hline 0&Z_D^\sigma\mathbb L_{i_0!}\mathbb L_{h_{0,*}} &c_D\mathbb L_{i_0!}\mathbb L_{h_{0,*}}\\ 1&Z_D^\sigma\mathbb L_{p_{0,*}}\mathbb L_{k_0!} &c_D\mathbb L_{p_{0,*}}\mathbb L_{k_0!}\\ 2&\mathbb L_{p_{2,*}}Z_C^\sigma\mathbb L_{k_0!} &\mathbb L_{p_{2,*}}c_C\mathbb L_{k_0!}\\ 3&\mathbb L_{p_{2,*}}\mathbb L_{k_2!}Z_U^\sigma &\mathbb L_{p_{2,*}}\mathbb L_{k_2!}c_U\\ 4&\mathbb L_{i_2!}Z_Y^\sigma\mathbb L_{h_{0,*}} &\mathbb L_{i_2!}c_Y\mathbb L_{h_{0,*}}\\ 5&\mathbb L_{i_2!}\mathbb L_{h_{2,*}}Z_U^\sigma &\mathbb L_{i_2!}\mathbb L_{h_{2,*}}c_U. \end{array}\tag{B.PR2} \] Retain all tensor associators and use the same \(c_T\) at every occurrence. All twelve words are whole h-projective in both endpoint variables, by the exterior-cell argument B.KC2.

There is one geometric receiving complex: \[ M(J,I)=\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet} \bigl(A_{D,2}A_{D,1}i_{0,!}h_{0,*}e_{U_0}I, e_{D_2}J\bigr). \tag{B.PR3} \] Define \(a_v^\sigma:W_v^\sigma\to M\) by the ordered augmentation formula B.MX4. For \(d\), use the displayed inverse-image isomorphism to identify its source with B.PR3. For \(o\), use successive proper and open base-change maps. These are maps of actual complexes: the proper comparison for the composite is the ordered comparison B.OD5, and the open comparison is B.OD7. These identities, together with naturality of the proper–open exchange, give the same six maps \(\tau_v\) into the corresponding geometric words. No equality of independently chosen kernel lifts is needed for that assertion.

Each \(a_v^\sigma\) is a whole quasi-isomorphism. For the direct words this is the six-case argument B.MX4. For the ordered words, replace the single exact inverse-image step in each of those cases by its two exact steps. In a kernel calculation reduce each such column through its homotopy equivalence to a corepresentable, in the order in which the two operations occur. Co-Yoneda then gives \(A_{T,2}A_{T,1}\). In the cases containing a subsequent proper image, choose the intermediate K-injective replacement before that image, just as in B.MX4; the equalities B.OD5 and B.OD7 identify the remaining map with the direct one. Thus the same six derived comparisons prove the assertion. This uses no preservation of an arbitrary quasi-isomorphism by a raw proper image.

Whisker the original homotopy of \(c_T\) through this augmentation. Naturality of the raw comparison maps gives \[ a_v^d C_v-a_v^o=d\eta_v,\qquad |\eta_v|=-1. \tag{B.PR4} \] Here \(\eta_v\) is that whiskered homotopy, including the Koszul sign when it occurs in a right tensor factor. The equality is obtained by applying the same balanced composition map used to define \(a_v^\sigma\) to B.OD3. It retains the specified compositor and its witness.

2. Six rectangles with both comparison coordinates

For an edge \(e=e_{ij}:j\to i\) in the reversed mixed index, keep \[ a_i^\sigma\lambda_e^\sigma-a_j^\sigma=d\omega_e^\sigma. \] On the ordered side the proper and open edges are the two successive block maps; the proper–open edges are those at rows zero and two, with the inverse-image factors retained. B.OD6 supplies the witnesses for a successive block. B.MX5 supplies the common-target witnesses after whiskering. Keep the existing mixed pairs \((H_\sigma,K_\sigma)\) as well: \[ dH_\sigma=T_\sigma-B_\sigma,\qquad a_0^\sigma H_\sigma-(\Omega_T^\sigma-\Omega_B^\sigma) =dK_\sigma. \tag{B.PR5} \] All symbols in this equation are defined by B.MX7–8 using the corresponding six edges.

Form the graph category B.MX9 over the single complex \(M\). Its closed edge and vertex-comparison arrows are \[ E_\sigma(e)=(1,\lambda_e^\sigma,\omega_e^\sigma),\qquad \gamma_v=(1,C_v,\eta_v), \] and its mixed arrow is \(E_\sigma(c)=(0,H_\sigma,K_\sigma)\). The difference \(E_d(e)\gamma_j-\gamma_iE_o(e)\) has base component zero. Its other components are \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta_e&=\lambda_e^d C_j-C_i\lambda_e^o,\\ R_e&=\omega_e^d C_j+\eta_j -\eta_i\lambda_e^o-\omega_e^o. \end{aligned}\tag{B.PR6} \] Differentiation gives \(d\Delta_e=0\) and \(dR_e=a_i^d\Delta_e\). The Hom kernel of the graph projection is the shifted cone of \(\operatorname{Hom}(W_j^o,a_i^d)\), hence acyclic by whole h-projectivity. It therefore supplies \[ dh_e=\Delta_e,\qquad a_i^dh_e-R_e=dq_e, \qquad |h_e|=-1,quad |q_e|=-2. \tag{B.PR7} \] Write \(t_e=(0,h_e,q_e)\). Thus \(Dt_e=E_d(e)\gamma_j-\gamma_iE_o(e)\). If a proper or open rectangle already has a pair from B.OD8–9 with these exact compositor and augmentation witnesses, retain that pair, with the sign prescribed by B.PR6. The lifting argument concerns only an unfilled rectangle. A pair with different receiving witnesses must first be compared in the full graph; its second component cannot simply be substituted for \(h_e\).

3. The comparison of the two mixed cells

For a path \(p\), extend the rectangle homotopy by \[ t(gf)=t(g)E_o(f)+(-1)^{|g|}E_d(g)t(f). \tag{B.PR8} \] For the upper three-edge path its two non-base coordinates are \[ \begin{aligned} u_T={}&h_{01}\lambda_{12}^o\lambda_{23}^o +\lambda_{01}^dh_{12}\lambda_{23}^o +\lambda_{01}^d\lambda_{12}^dh_{23},\\ v_T={}&q_{01}\lambda_{12}^o\lambda_{23}^o +(\omega_{01}^dh_{12}+q_{12})\lambda_{23}^o\\ &+(\omega_{01}^d\lambda_{12}^d+\omega_{12}^d)h_{23}+q_{23}. \end{aligned}\tag{B.PR9} \] The lower pair \((u_B,v_B)\) is obtained by replacing the ordered list \((01,12,23)\) by \((04,45,53)\) throughout this formula. Put \(u=u_T-u_B\), \(v=v_T-v_B\). These formulas follow from the full graph product; in particular the terms \(\omega^d h\) belong to the third coordinate.

The obstruction for the mixed generator is the literal graph element \[ E_d(c)\gamma_3-\gamma_0E_o(c)-t(dc)=(0,R,S), \] where \[ \begin{aligned} R&=H_dC_3-C_0H_o-u,\\ S&=K_dC_3-\eta_0H_o-K_o-v. \end{aligned}\tag{B.PR10} \] Its base component is zero because each mixed arrow has base zero, every compositor has base one, and each rectangle homotopy has base zero. This verifies the target before using acyclicity. By B.PR7–8, \[ dR=0,\qquad dS=a_0^dR. \tag{B.PR11} \] For example, differentiating \(t(dc)\) gives \(E_d(dc)\gamma_3-\gamma_0E_o(dc)\), since \(d^2c=0\). This cancels the derivative of the other two graph terms. The second equality in B.PR11 is the third coordinate of that graph identity.

The same whole Hom cone now supplies \[ dZ=R,\qquad a_0^dZ-S=dW, \qquad |Z|=-2,quad |W|=-3. \tag{B.PR12} \] Thus \(t_c=(0,Z,W)\) is the full comparison of the original mixed cells. Neither \(K_d,K_o\) nor the rectangle witnesses were changed to obtain it. The target in B.PR12 includes the original mixed witnesses, the compositor witness and all the terms in B.PR9.

Here is the precise parameter category. Start with disjoint direct and ordered copies of B.MP1's free index, including their generators \(c_d,c_o\). Adjoin closed arrows \(\gamma_v:v_o\to v_d\), then the degree-minus-one arrows \(t_e:j_o\to i_d\) with the B.PR7 boundary. Finally adjoin \(t_c:3_o\to0_d\), of degree minus two, with \[ dt_c=c_d\gamma_3-\gamma_0c_o-t(dc). \tag{B.PR13} \] In this presentation the letters denote formal generators and B.PR8 defines the formal path expression. The preceding cancellation proves that every assigned differential squares to zero. The order just given is a free cellular order: \(dt_e\) uses only edges and compositors, and \(dt_c\) uses only the two mixed generators and the earlier rectangles. Send every vertex to \(M\), every closed edge and compositor to \(1_M\), and every negative-degree generator to zero. This is a strict target diagram. B.PR4–12 give its strict lift to the graph category, relative to both supplied mixed diagrams.

4. The whole roof and the orientation of the right compositors

Let \(\mathcal J\) denote this free prism index and \(\mathcal W\) its diagram of whole left kernels. Apply the signed parameter-bar map B.MP4 on \(\mathcal J\). It is an actual quasi-isomorphism to the constant diagram \(M\). Its length-one values at a terminal identity include \[ \Psi(1\otimes t_e\otimes x)=-q_ex, \qquad \Psi(1\otimes t_c\otimes x)=-Wx. \tag{B.PR14} \] The second input has total degree \(|x|-3\), because \(|t_c|=-2\) and its bar length is one. Thus B.PR14 keeps the degree-minus-three witness as part of the strict map.

Resolve this entire bar diagram over \(\mathcal J\) times the endpoint product category. The ordinary bar augmentation gives a strict map \(p:R\to\mathcal W\). Each evaluated \(R_v\) is whole h-projective in the endpoint variables by B.ND6: the cellular path basis of \(\mathcal J\) gives the required semifree filtration. Each \(p_v\) is a quasi-isomorphism between whole h-projectives, hence a homotopy equivalence. Consequently \(Dp_v:D\mathcal W_v\to DR_v\) is a homotopy equivalence, without dualizing an arbitrary raw quasi-isomorphism. Keep the signed bar map to \(M\), its whole lift and both inverse witnesses exactly as in B.MP6–7. Restriction to a new index is followed by the B.CE11 re-resolution wherever whole projectivity is used.

The strict diagram \(N=DR\) is defined on \(\mathcal J^{\mathrm{op}}\). In right orientation let \(e^\sigma:i_\sigma\to j_\sigma\) be the reversed mixed edges, \(s_v:v_d\to v_o\) the compositor, and \(c^\sigma:0_\sigma\to3_\sigma\) the mixed generator. For the rectangles and prism use the negatives of the opposite \(t_e,t_c\). Their exact differential is \[ \begin{aligned} dt_e^r&=e^o s_i-s_j e^d,\\ dt_c^r&=c^o s_0-s_3c^d-t^r(T^r-B^r),\\ t^r(gf)&=t^r(g)f^d+(-1)^{|g|}g^o t^r(f). \end{aligned}\tag{B.PR15} \] Here \(T^r=e_{23}e_{12}e_{01}\) and \(B^r=e_{53}e_{45}e_{04}\). Reversing B.PR8 on these degree-zero paths gives \(t^r(p^{\mathrm{op}})=-t(p)^{\mathrm{op}}\); B.PR13 then gives the second equation. This checks the signs rather than identifying the two orientations informally.

The six maps have the intended geometric factorization. Write \[ r_T:P_{a_{T,21}}\longrightarrow P_{a_{T,1}}\otimes P_{a_{T,2}} \tag{B.PR16} \] for the actual direct-to-ordered right compositor, constructed through B.OD11's evaluation roof and its whole inverse with both homotopies. In the six right words B.FK1 the corresponding maps \(X_v:K_v^d\to K_v^o\) insert, respectively, \(r_D,r_D,r_C,r_U,r_Y,r_U\), retaining the other factors. For the standard compactification \(f_r=p_rk_r\), \[ X_1=H_{k_0}\otimes H_{p_0}\otimes r_D=vL_0, \qquad X_3=r_U\otimes H_{k_2}\otimes H_{p_2}=L_2s, \tag{B.PR17} \] where \(s=T_{r_U}\), \(v=T_{r_D}\); the equations mean the specified tensor functors with their canonical associators. The signed evaluations B.FK2–3 and the compositor roof give full witnesses \[ E_v^oX_v-(DC_v)E_v^d=dA_v^{\mathrm{cmp}}. \tag{B.PR18} \] Indeed the right compositor was obtained by lifting \(Dc_T\) through its receiving factor comparison. Whisker that lift equation with the unchanged factors and apply the closed evaluation B.RK3–4. The graded tensor rule gives B.PR18; it is the compositor version of B.FK5. Composing with \(Dp\) places these comparisons in the actual whole prism model, with their third coordinates retained.

B.PR13–18 specify the joint geometric parameter diagram and its factorized compositor maps. To use an independently prescribed right-word mixed cell or inverse homotopy, its full comparison with this whole prism is still required. B.WI17–18 measures the displacement of prescribed endpoint homotopies; B.PR12 does not assert that an arbitrary such displacement is exact. The RCmp target and mate construction must use the transported full records on this common index. Its higher triangle, all changing-array comparisons, nearby-cycle descent and normalized coefficient completion retain their respective hypotheses and proof obligations. \(\square\)

Construct the inertia quotient and its exact invariants

Here is the group input for every strictly henselian trait used above. Fix a uniformizer \(u\) and a compatible system of its roots. For an integer \(n\) prime to \(p\), the field \(K\) contains \(\mu_n\): the distinct residue roots lift by Hensel's lemma. The extension \(K(u^{1/n})/K\) is cyclic of degree \(n\). Its powers \(1,u^{1/n},\ldots,u^{(n-1)/n}\) are linearly independent because their valuations occupy distinct classes modulo \(\mathbf Z\); the defining polynomial gives the opposite degree inequality. Its value group is \(n^{-1}\mathbf Z\), and its residue field is unchanged. For the latter assertion, the terms in a basis expansion have distinct fractional valuations, so the least term determines the residue after division by an element of the same valuation.

Let \(K^t\) be the union of these extensions. Its value group is \(\mathbf Z[1/n:(n,p)=1]\), its residue field is separably closed, and \(\operatorname{Gal}(K^t/K)=\varprojlim_{(n,p)=1}\mu_n=\prod_{r\ne p}\mathbf Z_r(1)\). The field is henselian by Lemma A.1a and Theorem A.1b, which identify the extending valuation ring with the local henselian integral closure without assuming a finite normalization.

We verify that \(P=\operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{sep}}/K^t)\) is pro-\(p\), including when finite extensions have defect. For a prime \(r\ne p\), the value group of \(K^t\) is \(r\)-divisible. A finite-index enlargement \(\Gamma'\) of an \(r\)-divisible subgroup \(\Gamma\) in a torsion-free group is still \(r\)-divisible. In fact, \(r\gamma'\in\Gamma\) implies \(\gamma'\in\Gamma\), by dividing in \(\Gamma\) and using torsion-freeness. Hence the finite group \(\Gamma'/\Gamma\) has no \(r\)-torsion. Multiplication by \(r\) on that quotient is bijective; lift a division there and correct its error by division in \(\Gamma\).

Every finite extension of \(K^t\) has such a finite value-group index, by the distinct-value linear-independence argument in Appendix A, and has separably closed residue field. If a finite Galois extension had an automorphism of prime order \(r\ne p\), its fixed field would thus have \(r\)-divisible value group and separably closed residue field. Every nonzero element of that field is an \(r\)-th power: match its valuation, extract a root of the remaining residue unit, and lift by Hensel's lemma. It also contains \(\mu_r\). Diagonalizing the automorphism would produce a nontrivial eigenvector \(v\) with \(v^r\) in the fixed field. A root \(b\) of \(v^r\) there would imply \(v/b\in\mu_r\), contradicting the nontrivial eigenvalue. The finite-group argument proved in Appendix A now excludes every prime divisor other than \(p\) from each finite Galois quotient. When \(p=1\), it excludes every prime.

Over the strict trait full inertia is \(I=\operatorname{Gal}(K^{\mathrm{sep}}/K)\). Project the tame quotient to its \(\ell\)-factor and put

\[ H=\ker\bigl(I\longrightarrow\mathbf Z_\ell(1)\bigr). \tag{B.3} \]

Every finite quotient of \(H\) has order prime to \(\ell\): its normal wild image is a \(p\)-group and its remaining quotient comes from the other tame factors. Invariants on discrete \(\ell\)-primary modules are exact. To lift an invariant element through a surjection, lift it first arbitrarily, choose a finite quotient through which the orbit of this lift factors, and average over that quotient. Its order is invertible in the coefficients. Refining the quotient repeats every summand equally, so the average is independent of that choice and commutes with maps and restrictions.

These compatible averaging idempotents split the underlying sheaf and its complement. Stalks and costalks preserve the splitting, so both perverse support cuts are preserved as well. The normalized coefficient comparison carries this construction to adic complexes. Thus the resulting invariant functor is perverse t-exact and commutes with perverse cohomology; that normalized comparison is part of the stated formalism prerequisites.

The remaining quotient \(\Gamma=\mathbf Z_\ell(1)\) has cohomology only in degrees zero and one on discrete \(\ell\)-primary modules. We verify the continuous comparison directly. Choose a generator \(T\), put \(\Gamma_n=\ell^n\Gamma\), and first let \(M\) be killed by \(\ell^a\). A continuous cochain on \(\Gamma\) has finite image by compactness. For sufficiently large \(n\), it factors through \(\Gamma/\Gamma_n\) and its values lie in \(M^{\Gamma_n}\). Thus the continuous cochain complex is the filtered union of the finite cyclic group cochain complexes with these coefficient submodules; filtered unions commute with kernels and images.

For a cyclic group of order \(\ell^n\), the augmented free group-ring resolution alternates multiplication by \(T-1\) and by \(N_n=1+T+\cdots+T^{\ell^n-1}\). Its exactness is a coefficient calculation: the kernel of \(T-1\) consists of constant coefficient vectors, the image of \(N_n\); the kernel of \(N_n\) consists of coefficient vectors of sum zero, the image of \(T-1\). For the quotient from order \(\ell^{n+1}\) to order \(\ell^n\), inflation is represented in resolution degree \(q\) by projection multiplied by \(\ell^{\lfloor q/2\rfloor}\). This is a chain map because projection sends \(N_{n+1}\) to \(\ell N_n\) and preserves \(T-1\). Consequently every class in degree \(q\geq2\) dies after at most \(a\) successive inflations. In degree one, any \(v\in M\) eventually belongs to \(\ker N_n\): if its orbit has period dividing \(\ell^r\), then \(N_nv=\ell^{n-r}N_rv=0\) for \(n\geq r+a\). We obtain

\[ H^0(\Gamma,M)=\ker(T-1),\qquad H^1(\Gamma,M)=M/(T-1)M,\qquad H^q(\Gamma,M)=0\quad(q\geq2). \]

The natural two-term comparison sends its degree-zero element to the corresponding zero-cochain and its degree-one element \(v\) to the continuous crossed homomorphism with value \(v\) at \(T\), constructed in Appendix C. The coboundary of a zero-cochain has value \((T-1)v\), so this is a chain map; the calculation above proves it a quasi-isomorphism. Taking the union of the submodules killed by \(\ell^a\) proves the claim for every discrete \(\ell\)-primary module. Together with exact \(H\)-invariants this proves \(\operatorname{cd}_\ell K\leq1\), including for the fields \(K_d\) above. The application to equivariant sheaves and normalized adic coefficients still requires their stated descent and coefficient comparisons.

The étale proof keeps full inertia

Let \(M\) be perverse for the shifted generic convention, and set \(C=R\psi M\) and \(B=i^*Rj_*M\). On pointed neighborhoods the geometric generic Galois cover, its augmentation and continuous descent give

\[ B=R\Gamma(I,C)=R\Gamma(\mathbf Z_\ell(1),C^H). \tag{B.4} \]

This identity is compatible with the augmentation \(B\to C\). Exact invariants, the length-one resolution and boundedness allow passage through the pointed filtered limit. After choosing \(T\) and forgetting residue-field descent, it becomes

\[ B\simeq\operatorname{Fib}(T-1:C^H\longrightarrow C^H). \tag{B.5} \]

The two copies have the same underlying sheaf. Their intrinsic arithmetic descent structures differ by the Iwasawa functor constructed in Appendix C. A uniform identification with an ordinary Tate twist is not used here.

The localization triangle \(j_!M\to Rj_*M\to i_*B\) and Lemma B.1 put \(B\) in perverse degrees \([-1,0]\). The long exact sequence of (B.5) makes \(T-1\) surjective on \({}^pH^q(C^H)\) for \(q\geq0\), and injective for \(q\leq-2\). To exploit these statements we must justify both the eigenvalue decomposition and the permitted twists.

For a constructible perverse object \(A\), its algebra \(\operatorname{End}(A)\) is finite dimensional over \(E\). The exact finiteness input \(H^0(X_s,R\mathcal Hom(A,A))\) is proved for entire derived objects by Lemma B.0, from the complete integral Hom complex and its rationalization. Its finite-stage argument also supplies continuity of the actual nearby action, subject to the separately recorded nearby constructibility hypothesis. The argument uses those operation theorems with their stated geometric and coefficient hypotheses. The automorphism \(T\) therefore satisfies a polynomial. After a finite coefficient extension, factor its minimal polynomial as \(\prod_\lambda(x-\lambda)^{m_\lambda}\). Bézout identities for these relatively prime factors give orthogonal polynomial idempotents adding to one. Their images split \(A\) in the abelian perverse heart, and \(T-\lambda\) is nilpotent on the corresponding image. There are finitely many nonzero perverse cohomology objects, so one finite coefficient extension suffices for all of them. This argument does not require an injective resolution inside constructible sheaves or a Jordan decomposition of the entire derived object.

Each eigenvalue gives a continuous character of \(\mathbf Z_\ell(1)\). Here are the topological details. Left multiplication embeds the unit group of \(\operatorname{End}(A)\) faithfully in the linear automorphisms of that finite-dimensional algebra. The given continuous action has \(T^{\ell^n}\to1\), so its eigenvalues satisfy \(\lambda^{\ell^n}\to1\) in a finite coefficient extension. Compactness of all integer powers makes \(\lambda\) a unit. If an integer difference is divisible by \(\ell^n\), the corresponding powers of \(\lambda\) differ by at most \(|\lambda^{\ell^n}-1|\): use the geometric sum for positive powers and the unit inverse for negative powers. Thus \(a\mapsto\lambda^a\) on \(\mathbf Z\) is uniformly continuous for the \(\ell\)-adic topology. Completeness extends it uniquely to a continuous homomorphism on \(\mathbf Z_\ell\). Sending \(T\) to \(\lambda^{-1}\) gives the required inverse character.

Pull this rank-one local system back from the generic point of the strict trait and tensor it with \(M\). At finite coefficient levels a finite free local system is étale locally constant, and the stalk and costalk tensor comparisons follow there. The normalized coefficient comparisons give those maps for \(E\); tensoring either test with a finite-dimensional fibre preserves its vanishing, so tensoring is t-exact. After passage to the geometric generic point, the parameter system is constant; the construction of nearby cycles gives the coefficient tensor identity with its descent action. On \(H\)-invariants the twist replaces \(T\) by \(\lambda^{-1}T\). The preceding surjectivity or injectivity therefore applies to a nilpotent operator on each forbidden-degree eigencomponent. A nilpotent monomorphism or epimorphism forces its object to be zero, by iterating to the zero power. Faithful scalar extension detects that zero before the coefficient extension. We obtain

\[ C^H[-1]\in\operatorname{Perv}(X_s). \tag{B.6} \]

The parameter characters exist on the strict generic point itself. No extension to a chosen arithmetic Frobenius, or geometric-origin condition on the original complex, was needed for this step.

Recover the full inertia object from a finite regular representation

We now detect what \(H\)-invariants alone might lose. For each nonzero \(A_q={}^pH^qC\), use the faithful linear action on \(\operatorname{End}(A_q)\) just described. A continuous compact group action on a finite-dimensional \(E\)-space preserves a lattice. Indeed, the matrices of its compact image have uniformly bounded entries. The sum of the translates of any initial lattice lies in one fixed larger lattice, contains the initial lattice, and is finitely generated over the valuation ring; it is the required invariant lattice.

The kernel of reduction on the automorphisms of that lattice is pro-\(\ell\). Its filtration by matrices congruent to one modulo successive powers of the uniformizer has finite additive residue-field quotients and trivial intersection. The image of \(H\) is pro-prime-to-\(\ell\), and its closed subgroups have the same property: any finite quotient of a closed subgroup is detected inside a finite quotient of the original profinite group. Its intersection with that pro-\(\ell\) kernel is therefore trivial. Consequently the kernel of the finite residue representation of \(I\), when intersected with \(H\), acts trivially on \(A_q\). Combine the finitely many residue representations to obtain a finite quotient \(Q\) of \(I\) with this property for every \(q\).

Let \(\rho=E[Q]\) with its regular left action. It defines a finite parameter local system on the strict generic point. Geometric-generic pullback trivializes it, so the finite direct-sum coefficient comparison gives

\[ R\psi(M\otimes f^*\rho)=C\otimes\rho \tag{B.7} \]

with the diagonal descent action. Apply (B.6) to this new perverse input. Thus \((C\otimes\rho)^H\) has only perverse degree \(-1\).

Let \(J\) be the image of \(H\) in \(Q\). The \(H\)-action on each \(A_q\) factors through \(J\). For a single regular copy there is an explicit isomorphism of underlying perverse objects

\[ A_q\longrightarrow (A_q\otimes E[J])^J, \qquad x\longmapsto\sum_{h\in J}h x\otimes e_h. \]

The inverse extracts the coefficient of \(e_1\). Invariance says that the coefficient of \(e_h\) must be \(h\) times that coefficient, proving both inverse identities. The displayed notation is a finite matrix of actual morphisms in the additive category, so it detects the whole perverse object, including its attaching maps. Restriction of \(E[Q]\) to \(J\) is the direct sum of these regular copies, one for each left coset. Hence the twisted-invariant functor is faithful on the \(A_q\). Exact invariants and finite coefficient tensoring commute with perverse cohomology. Their vanishing in every degree except \(-1\) forces

\[ R\psi M[-1]\in\operatorname{Perv}(X_s) \quad\text{with full continuous inertia}. \tag{B.8} \]

Thus the conclusion concerns the original nearby object, including its wild and prime-to-\(\ell\) tame actions.

Use the augmentation to handle vanishing cycles

Write \(E_M=R\psi M[-1]\). The normalized specialization fibre gives \(\Phi(j_!M)=E_M\), since the special restriction of \(j_!M\) is zero. For a closed-supported object it gives \(\Phi(i_*A)=A\). To pass from these cases to every perverse object we need the map between them, not only their isomorphism classes.

Localization gives \(i^!j_!M=B[-1]=R\Gamma(I,E_M)\). The two-term resolution and exact \(H\)-invariants put this costalk in perverse degrees \([0,1]\), with degree-zero object \(E_M^I\). A morphism from a perverse \(A\) into it factors uniquely through that degree-zero truncation, by the two orthogonality vanishings in its truncation triangle. Accordingly adjunction identifies a heart morphism \(i_*A\to j_!M\) with \(A\to E_M^I\). Under \(\Phi\) its map is

\[ A\longrightarrow E_M^I\hookrightarrow E_M. \tag{B.9} \]

To verify this last identification, apply the enhanced specialization fibre to the localization triangle \(i_*B[-1]\to j_!M\to Rj_*M\). For \(Rj_*M\), specialization is the augmentation \(B=R\Gamma(I,C)\to C\) of (B.4). Taking the corresponding fibres and rotating gives \(B[-1]\to C[-1]\to\operatorname{Cone}(B\to C)[-1]\), whose first map is that same augmentation shifted. In perverse degree zero it is exactly \(E_M^I\hookrightarrow E_M\). Naturality and adjunction give (B.9) for every \(A\). The enhanced attaching homotopy is retained in this calculation; an unenhanced square of zero stalk maps would not determine it.

If \(i_*A\to j_!M\) is monic in the heart, its adjoint \(A\to E_M^I\) is monic too: a kernel would push forward to a subobject killed by the original monomorphism. Hence (B.9) is monic. For any perverse \(K\), set \(M=j^*K\) and factor the heart counit through its image \(J_K\):

\[ 0\longrightarrow i_*A\longrightarrow j_!M\longrightarrow J_K\longrightarrow0, \qquad 0\longrightarrow J_K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow i_*D\longrightarrow0. \]

The kernel and cokernel are closed-supported because their generic restrictions vanish. Applying \(\Phi\) to the first triangle gives a monomorphism \(A\to E_M\) of perverse objects, so its cone \(\Phi J_K\) is perverse. The second triangle then makes \(\Phi K\) an extension of \(\Phi J_K\) by \(D\), hence perverse. Finite perverse truncation triangles now prove both cuts for \(\Psi\) and \(\Phi\) on bounded complexes: each complex is a finite extension of its shifted perverse cohomology objects, and the functors preserve the heart and shifts. They are therefore t-exact and exact on the hearts.

For a non-strict henselian trait, pull back to its strict localization for these tests; faithfully forgetting residue-field descent detects the two cuts. With the total-space convention, \(\Psi_fK=R\psi(j^*K)[-1]\); for a usual generic-fibre perverse input \(L\), the assertion reads \(R\psi L\) perverse. Finite coefficient descent and faithful extension give \(\overline{\mathbf Q}_\ell\).

The full assigned arbitrary-trait statements are thus reduced to explicit foundations, including the ordinary affine and constructible-finiteness theorems, strict-local continuity, henselian valuation extension, trait purity and duality, the continuous sheaf-descent comparison, and normalized adic reduction and rationalization. Their exact recursive proofs remain required. This argument does not use a nearby- or vanishing-cycle duality theorem; the separate comparisons are developed in Appendices D and E.

Appendix C. Full étale variation and the Iwasawa twist

The variation target must carry the arithmetic action, as well as the operator seen after choosing a geometric inertia generator. We construct that target from continuous crossed homomorphisms, prove the change-of-generator and group-algebra statements, and then obtain variation from the actual specialization map. For the Iwasawa twist and its sheaf version, see Lu–Zheng, arXiv version 7. The full sliced-topos duality theorem is a separate result; the construction here does not assume it.

Construct the target before choosing its coordinates

Keep \(H=\ker(I\to\mathbf Z_\ell(1))\) from Appendix B and put \(\Gamma=I/H\). Exact averaging gives

\[ V=V^H\oplus V^{\mathrm{rest}}. \tag{C.1} \]

The second summand has zero \(H\)-invariants. We will leave it unchanged. On \(V^H\) write \(G=G_\eta/H\); then \(\Gamma\) is a normal subgroup of \(G\), and conjugation is \(gTg^{-1}=T^{\chi(g)}\) for a geometric generator \(T\) and the cyclotomic character \(\chi\). No splitting of \(G\to G_s\) is needed.

Begin with a finite coefficient ring \(\Lambda=O/\pi^m\), annihilated by some power \(\ell^a\). For a discrete continuous \(G\)-module \(M\), let \(Z^1(\Gamma,M)\) consist of continuous maps satisfying

\[ c(xy)=c(x)+x\,c(y), \qquad (g c)(x)=g\,c(g^{-1}xg). \]

This definition is independent of a generator. Evaluation at \(T\) identifies its underlying coefficient module with \(M\). Here is the existence and continuity argument. Given \(v\in M\), a cocycle must have \(c(T^n)=\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}T^iv\) for positive integers \(n\), and its values at negative powers follow from \(c(1)=0\). The orbit of \(v\) has a period dividing \(\ell^r\), since a compact pro-\(\ell\) group acts continuously on a discrete set. Hence the displayed sum over \(\ell^{r+a}\) terms is zero, and \(T^{\ell^{r+a}}\) fixes the cyclic submodule generated by \(v\). The formula therefore defines a cocycle on the finite cyclic quotient of that order, then a continuous cocycle on \(\Gamma\). Uniqueness follows because the integer powers of \(T\) are dense and \(M\) is discrete.

Put \(t=T-1\), and for \(b\in\mathbf Z_\ell^\times\) define

\[ u_b(t)=\frac{(1+t)^b-1}{t} =b+\binom b2t+\binom b3t^2+\cdots. \]

These series act on discrete torsion modules. On the cyclic submodule of a section with period \(\ell^r\), the relation \((1+t)^{\ell^r}=1\) implies \(t^{\ell^r}\in\ell\Lambda[t]\), so \(t^{a\ell^r}\) acts by zero. Only finitely many terms matter there. The constant term of \(u_b\) is a unit, so its inverse is obtained recursively, or by a finite geometric series on each such submodule. The integer sum formula and continuity give \(c(T^b)=u_b(t)c(T)\).

In these coordinates the action on \(Z^1(\Gamma,M)\) is

\[ g\star_-v=u_{\chi(g)}(t)^{-1}g v. \]

Indeed its original expression is \(g\,u_{\chi(g)^{-1}}(t)v\). Moving the series through \(g\), and using \(((1+t)^{\chi(g)})^{\chi(g)^{-1}}=1+t\), gives the displayed inverse. The opposite action \(g\star_+v=u_{\chi(g)}(t)g v\) defines an inverse functor. To check the group law explicitly, put \(t_b=(1+t)^b-1\); then

\[ u_{bc}(t)=u_b(t)u_c(t_b). \]

For positive integers this follows by factoring \((1+t)^{bc}-1\) twice; continuity gives it for \(b,c\in\mathbf Z_\ell^\times\). Since \(g f(t)=f(t_{\chi(g)})g\), this identity verifies both action laws. Both actions leave the operator \(T\) unchanged, so composing them cancels the two units. They are exact inverse functors on coefficient modules and on equivariant sheaves, where the formulas apply to sections and commute with restriction. In particular their underlying sheaves and perverse degrees are unchanged.

Changing the generator to \(T^b\) replaces the cocycle coordinate by multiplication by \(u_b(t)\). This is an invertible, natural comparison. For the positive functor the comparison in the reverse direction is multiplication by the same unit; the displayed product identity verifies its equivariance and the compatibility of successive changes. Thus the functors are intrinsic, despite these useful coordinates.

Identify the invertible augmentation ideal

We also prove the group-algebra description, including the point that does not follow just from a one-variable power-series calculation. Let \(R=\varprojlim_N\Lambda[G/N]\), over open normal subgroups \(N\) of \(G\). Multiplication by \(t\) is injective on either side of \(R\).

For left multiplication, suppose \(tr=0\). At any finite quotient, the coefficients of \(r_N\) are constant along left \(T\)-orbits. Fix \(N\), and choose \(N'\subset N\) such that \([\Gamma\cap N \mathbin{:} \Gamma\cap N']\) is divisible by \(\ell^a\). Such subgroups exist because the topology induced on the closed subgroup \(\Gamma\) is its profinite topology: an arbitrarily small open subgroup of \(\Gamma\) contains \(\Gamma\cap N'\) for a sufficiently small open normal \(N'\) of \(G\). The fibre over any coset of \(G/N\) is partitioned by the left action of \(\Gamma\cap N\) into orbits of precisely that index; normality of \(N'\) gives the stated stabilizer. Coefficients are constant on each orbit, so their sum is zero in \(\Lambda\). The transition map consequently sends \(r_{N'}\) to zero. Hence \(r_N=0\) for every \(N\), proving \(r=0\). Right orbits prove right injectivity in the same way.

Conjugation gives \(gt=t\,u_{\chi(g)}(t)g\) and \(tg=u_{\chi(g)}(t)^{-1}gt\). Therefore \(J=tR=Rt\). These identities first give the two inclusions on finite linear combinations of group elements, then on their completion: \(R\) is compact, the multiplication maps are continuous, and their images are closed. Replacing \(T\) by \(T^b\) multiplies its generator by the unit \(u_b(t)\), so \(J\) is independent of that choice.

Every \(r\in R\) has a unique \(\beta(r)\) with \(rt=t\beta(r)\). Injectivity just proved shows that \(\beta\) preserves addition, multiplication and the identity. The reverse equality \(tR=Rt\) gives its inverse. For a group element, \(\beta(g)=u_{\chi(g)}(t)g\). Thus the two free rank-one module structures on \(J\) differ by this actual algebra automorphism. Tensoring with \(J\) twists the action by \(\beta\), while \(\operatorname{Hom}_R(J,-)\) twists it by \(\beta^{-1}\); their evaluations are inverse. This proves invertibility as a bimodule, not merely freeness on one side.

On the full inertia object the resulting functors are

\[ \tau V=(J\otimes_R V^H)\oplus V^{\mathrm{rest}}, \qquad \tau^{-1}V=\operatorname{Hom}_R(J,V^H)\oplus V^{\mathrm{rest}}. \tag{C.2} \]

The negative functor on \(V^H\) is the intrinsic crossed-homomorphism construction above: an \(R\)-linear map \(J\to V^H\) is determined by its value at \(t\), and its induced action is \(\star_-\). The same formulas at all coefficient quotients are compatible with reduction. Inverse limits give them on coefficient lattices, and rationalization gives the finite \(E/\mathbf Q_\ell\) version. A change between commensurable lattices gives the same rationalized maps. Passing these coefficient calculations through the normalized constructible adic sheaf category still requires the completeness, reduction and operation comparisons identified in Appendix A; this algebra calculation does not prove that formalism.

The differential and the variation triangle

There is a natural morphism \(\iota:V\to\tau^{-1}V\). On \(V^H\) it sends \(v\) to the crossed homomorphism \(x\mapsto xv-v\); on \(V^{\mathrm{rest}}\) it is the identity. Its coordinate on the first summand is \(t\), but its target carries the action \(\star_-\), which is needed for arithmetic equivariance.

The continuous group resolution and geometric-generic descent used in Appendix B now give the invariant form of its two-term complex:

\[ R\Gamma(I,V)=\operatorname{Fib}(\iota:V\to\tau^{-1}V). \tag{C.3} \]

Here the left side is viewed back in the equivariant category by pullback from the residue-field category. More explicitly, exact \(H\)-invariants reduce to \(\Gamma\), whose augmented completed-group resolution is multiplication by \(t\) on \(\Lambda[[t]]\), followed by evaluation at \(t=0\). Injectivity and the description of its cokernel prove exactness of that resolution. Applying the continuous coefficient Hom gives the two terms and the differential above; the crossed-homomorphism description supplies their descent action. On the complementary summand, derived \(H\)-invariants vanish and the identity differential gives a contractible complex. This is compatible with the augmentation to \(V\), not just with the cohomology groups. The equivariant sheaf and adic interpretation uses the actual continuous-descent comparison of Appendix B and its stated foundations.

Its degree-zero cohomology is \(V^I\). The degree-one cohomology is \(V_I(-1)\): quotienting by \(t\) makes \(u_{\chi(g)}(t)^{-1}\) equal to \(\chi(g)^{-1}\), and the complementary \(H\)-coinvariants vanish by averaging. Thus the Tate factor on degree one follows from the action on the second term.

Proposition C.1 (full variation triangle). The normalized full cycles admit a natural triangle

\[ i^!K\longrightarrow\Phi_fK \xrightarrow{\mathrm{var}}\tau^{-1}\Psi_fK \longrightarrow i^!K[1], \tag{C.4} \]

and \(\mathrm{var}\,\mathrm{can}=\iota\).

Proof. Retain the enhanced attaching map \(a:A=i^*K\to B=i^*Rj_*j^*K\) and put \(C=R\psi j^*K\). Localization identifies \(\operatorname{Fib}(a)=i^!K\); specialization is \(A\to B\to C\). Equation (C.3) identifies \(B\to C\) with the augmentation and its cofiber with \(\tau^{-1}C\). Pasting the two composable maps gives the triangle of fibres

\[ \operatorname{Fib}(A\to B)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Fib}(A\to C)\longrightarrow \operatorname{Fib}(B\to C)\longrightarrow. \]

The three terms are respectively \(i^!K\), \(\Phi_fK\), and \(\tau^{-1}C[-1]=\tau^{-1}\Psi_fK\). On the common cone model the composite out of \(C[-1]\) is the differential \(\iota[-1]\), giving the claimed identity with the course sign \(T-1\). The maps and their homotopies come from the same augmentation and attaching map, so this is a natural triangle. \(\square\)

For perverse \(K\), once Appendix B's full nearby-cycle bound is available, (C.4) also proves the lower bound for \(\Phi_fK\): its first and third terms are lower-perverse. The specialization triangle gives the upper bound. This consequence retains the operation and constructibility prerequisites of that appendix.

When a Tate twist suffices, and when it fails

Over a characteristic-zero coefficient field, let \(t\) be nilpotent and put \(c(t)=\log(1+t)/t=1-t/2+t^2/3-\cdots\), a finite invertible series. Multiplication by \(c(t)\) gives an isomorphism \(V(1)\to\tau V\) on the unipotent tame part. Its equivariance follows from

\[ c(t_b)=\frac{b\,c(t)}{u_b(t)}, \qquad u_{\chi(g)}(t)g\,c(t)=\chi(g)c(t)g. \]

The first identity follows by taking the finite formal logarithm of \((1+t)^b\), initially for integers and then by continuity. The second is exactly the intertwining equation for \(\star_+\) and the Tate action. On a part where \(t\) is invertible, the map induced by \(J\hookrightarrow R\) instead identifies \(\tau V\) with \(V\): in coordinates it is multiplication by \(t\). On \(V^{\mathrm{rest}}\) the functor was already the identity.

There is a concrete torsion obstruction to replacing \(\tau\) uniformly by \((1)\). Take coefficients \(\mathbf F_2\), a two-dimensional space with \(N\ne0\), \(N^2=0\), and tame generator \(T=1+N\). Let an arithmetic element \(g\) have \(\chi(g)=3\) and act as the identity on that space. This satisfies the required relation because \(T^3=T\); it gives a continuous representation of the corresponding tame semidirect group. The usual Tate action of \(g\) is still the identity modulo two. But

\[ u_3(N)=3+3N+N^2=1+N, \]

so its action on \(\tau V\) is nontrivial. No intertwining isomorphism can conjugate an identity operator to that operator. Thus these two twists are not isomorphic in this example. The field logarithm comparison and the full torsion Iwasawa construction must remain distinct; neither establishes the additional torsion sliced-duality theorem.

Appendix D. Generic nearby-cycle duality

Nearby duality must compare the actual evaluation pairings, not just the dimensions of the resulting groups. We first define its comparison using the exceptional-pushforward counit. We then test that map on coordinate generic fibres and on proper global cohomology. The permitted primary source is Illusie's Theorem 4.2, construction 4.3 and Variant 4.4, in the freely readable Numdam edition; the auxiliary field and finite-support arguments are supplied in Appendix A. Lu–Zheng's free text distinguishes this generic-fibre theorem from the larger sliced duality theorem used for general torsion coefficients.

Proposition D.1. Let \(X/S\) be separated of finite type over a henselian discrete valuation trait, with \(\ell\) invertible on \(S\), and let \(L\in D_c^b(X_\eta,E)\), for a finite extension \(E/\mathbf Q_\ell\). With the ordinary duality, base-change and normalized coefficient foundations specified below, there is a natural isomorphism

\[ \beta_{X,L}:R\psi(D_{X_\eta}L)\xrightarrow{\sim} D_{X_s}(R\psi L). \tag{D.1} \]

Both dualizing complexes are relative to their respective fields. The special object retains its full inertia action and residue-field descent. The comparison and its dimension argument below use the specified ordinary and adic operations.

Define the comparison by evaluation and counit

Write \(a_\eta:X_\eta\to\eta\) and \(a_s:X_s\to s\), and set \(\omega_\eta=a_\eta^!E\), \(\omega_s=a_s^!E\). For a separated finite-type map \(h:X\to Y\) over the trait, the ordinary operations give a natural transformation

\[ \alpha_h:Rh_{s!}R\psi_X\longrightarrow R\psi_YRh_{\eta!}. \]

Here is the construction needed in this proof. For an open immersion \(u\), smooth base change identifies \(u_s^*R\psi_Yu_{\eta!}\) with \(R\psi_X\). Take the adjoint of that identity under \(u_{s!}\dashv u_s^*\). For a proper map \(p\), take the proper base-change isomorphism. For a factorization \(h=p u\), compose \(Rp_{s*}\alpha_u\) with that proper comparison. On a common compactification, the proper comparisons compose and the open comparisons have the same adjoint identity. The triangle identities for the two adjunctions therefore identify the composites. This also proves compatibility with a further proper map. The compactification and ordinary operation-coherence statements required here are part of the earlier six-operation foundations; affine charts in the induction admit projective closures directly.

Apply \(\alpha_h\) to \(h_\eta^!N\), follow it by the exceptional-pushforward counit, and take the adjoint under \(Rh_{s!}\dashv h_s^!\). This gives

\[ R\psi_Xh_\eta^!N\longrightarrow h_s^!R\psi_YN. \]

For the structure map and \(N=E_\eta\), use \(R\psi_SE_\eta=E_s\). The latter identity is the cohomology of the separably closed geometric generic point of the strict trait. We obtain a specified map \(\theta_X:R\psi\omega_\eta\to\omega_s\).

The tensor comparison for nearby cycles is the adjoint of tensoring the pullback counits on the geometric generic fibre. It is the usual cup product on the same cochain construction. Compose it with evaluation and \(\theta_X\):

\[ R\psi L\otimes R\psi(D_{X_\eta}L) \longrightarrow R\psi(L\otimes D_{X_\eta}L) \longrightarrow R\psi\omega_\eta \xrightarrow{\theta_X}\omega_s. \]

Adjunction for internal Hom defines \(\beta_{X,L}\). Thus its normalization is fixed by the ordinary trace; we have not chosen an unspecified scalar multiple of a pairing.

We will use two compatibilities of this construction. Under proper pushforward, the resulting pairing is the pairing of the pushed-forward complex followed by its trace. Before taking adjoints, the verification is the counit identity \(\epsilon_{gh}=\epsilon_g\circ Rg_!(\epsilon_h)\) and the composition identity for \(\alpha\); the tensor counits used in evaluation obey the same identity. Under open restriction, both comparisons have the identity as their adjoint, so restriction preserves \(\beta\). Smooth purity similarly preserves the evaluation after inserting its relative dualizing line. Finite-presentation continuity gives the corresponding identifications through the pointed étale limits used next. These checks use the actual base-change and duality maps, not merely isomorphism classes of complexes.

Compare the two dualizing lines on a coordinate fibre

Pass to a strict localization of the base, and let \(k\) be its separably closed residue field. Faithful restriction will later detect an isomorphism with descent. On an affine chart choose a coordinate map \(f:X\to\mathbb A^1_S\). Let \(S_t\) be the auxiliary strict trait of Appendix A and put \(Y=X\times_{\mathbb A^1_S}S_t\). Denote the generic and special restriction maps by \(q_\eta\) and \(q_s\), and set \(L'=q_\eta^*L\).

The factor in the duality comparison comes from the affine line, not from a choice of inertia generator. Factor the structure map of \(X_\eta\) through \(\mathbb A^1_K\). The composition of exceptional inverse images and smooth purity give \(\omega_{X_\eta/K}=f_\eta^!E_{\mathbb A^1_K}(1)[2]\). Restricting to the coordinate generic field and using ordinary exceptional base change therefore gives

\[ q_\eta^*D_{X_\eta}L \simeq D_{Y_{\eta_t}}L'(1)[2]. \]

The same factorization over \(k\), with \(\mathbb A^1_k\) in place of \(\mathbb A^1_K\), gives for a constructible complex \(M\) on \(X_s\)

\[ q_s^*D_{X_s}M \simeq D_{Y_{s_t}}(q_s^*M)(1)[2]. \]

These are identifications from the same smooth-line trace orientation. At each finite pointed neighborhood they follow from the ordinary purity and exceptional-base-change maps; constructible continuity passes them to the generic-field limit. Consequently the factor \((1)[2]\) occurs on both sides of the desired comparison.

Appendix A proved that \(K'=\bar K\otimes_KK_t\) is a field and that \(P=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{K_t}/K')\) is pro-\(p\). Its comparison (A.1) identifies \(q_s^*R\psi_SL\) with \((R\psi_{S_t}L')^P\). Averaging commutes with duality by an explicit pairing calculation. For a finite quotient acting on coefficients, let \(e=|P_0|^{-1}\sum_{g\in P_0}g\). Contragredient evaluation satisfies \(\langle gv,w\rangle=\langle v,g^{-1}w\rangle\); replacing \(g\) by \(g^{-1}\) in the sum gives \(\langle ev,w\rangle=\langle v,ew\rangle\). Thus \(e\) is self-adjoint, its two images are orthogonal complements, and \(D(N^P)\simeq(DN)^P\). The compatible projectors at finite coefficient levels give the adic statement under the recorded normalization comparison. The auxiliary \(P\) acts trivially on the prime-to-\(p\) Tate line, whose roots of unity already lie in the strictly henselian base field.

Combining these identities, the source and target of \(q_s^*\beta_{X,L}\) identify respectively with

\[ \bigl(R\psi_{S_t}D_{Y_{\eta_t}}L'\bigr)^P(1)[2], \qquad \bigl(D_{Y_{s_t}}R\psi_{S_t}L'\bigr)^P(1)[2]. \]

Under these identifications its map is \((\beta_{Y,L'})^P(1)[2]\). To check the map, restrict the defining evaluation-and-counit composite: both exceptional base-change identifications insert the same line trace, and the self-adjoint projector restricts that evaluation to the invariant summands. Its tensor and counit composites are exactly those defining \(\beta_{Y,L'}\). In particular this comparison uses the canonical augmentation and trace maps rather than an arbitrary isomorphism between the displayed objects.

Eliminate the comparison cone by dimension and proper cohomology

Induct on \(n=\dim X_\eta\), beginning with \(X_\eta=\varnothing\). In that initial case both sides of (D.1) are zero. Nearby constructibility from Appendix A and ordinary Verdier constructibility make the cone \(C\) of \(\beta_{X,L}\) bounded constructible. Take this cone in the same enhanced sheaf category as its defining maps.

The coordinate-family dimension calculation of Appendix A applies to each affine chart. A component with nonconstant coordinate loses one transcendence degree; a component with algebraic coordinate disappears over the coordinate fraction field. Hence \(\dim Y_{\eta_t}<n\) whenever that generic fibre is nonempty. The induction hypothesis and the preceding map comparison show \(q_s^*C=0\) for every coordinate. When \(n=0\), all these coordinate generic fibres are empty, so the same initial case applies. No assertion that the original special fibre is zero dimensional is needed.

If a cohomology sheaf of \(C\) had a positive-dimensional support stratum in an affine chart, some coordinate would be nonconstant on its irreducible closure. Its nonzero generic germ would survive on the corresponding coordinate generic fibre, contradicting \(q_s^*C=0\). A finite constructible stratification therefore leaves only finitely many closed points in the support. Boundedness gives one finite set for all the cohomology sheaves of \(C\).

We may now prove that \(C\) vanishes on an arbitrary affine chart by embedding that chart into a projective \(S\)-scheme and extending its generic complex by zero. Its restriction back to the chart is the original comparison, by the open compatibility above. The generic dimension has not increased. Run the same coordinate test on affine charts of this projective closure; its comparison cone again has finite closed-point support. Thus it suffices to consider projective \(X/S\).

Proper base change and ordinary proper duality identify the global comparison with

\[ R\Gamma(X_{\bar\eta},D_{X_{\bar\eta}}L_{\bar\eta}) \longrightarrow D_E R\Gamma(X_{\bar\eta},L_{\bar\eta}), \qquad D_E=R\operatorname{Hom}_E(-,E). \]

This is the ordinary proper-duality isomorphism: the compatibility already checked identifies its pairing with evaluation followed by the proper trace. On the target we also used ordinary proper duality on \(X_s\) and proper base change for \(R\psi L\). It follows that \(R\Gamma(X_s,C)=0\).

Finally, a constructible cohomology sheaf supported on finitely many closed points over a separably closed field is the finite sum of its skyscrapers. Those points have purely inseparable residue extensions and no positive étale cohomology, as in Appendix A. The bounded cohomology spectral sequence therefore identifies \(H^qR\Gamma(X_s,C)=\bigoplus_x H^q(C_x)\). The left side is zero, so every geometric stalk of \(C\) is zero and \(C=0\). This proves the induction and the local comparisons, which glue by their common evaluation-and-counit construction. Faithful restriction from the original trait to its strict localization detects the isomorphism, while the natural maps retain full inertia and residue-field descent. \(\square\)

The outstanding inputs are exact ordinary compactification and six-operation coherence, proper and smooth base change, exceptional base change and purity with the stated trace orientation, constructible duality and proper finiteness, the continuous geometric-generic comparison, and normalized adic reduction and rationalization. These are hypotheses of the stated deduction. The \(P\)-invariants in the induction concern only the auxiliary coordinate field; they do not replace the final full-inertia object by tame cycles.

Appendix E. Duality of the full specialization cone

The algebra of dual cones depends on a differential, an augmentation and the homotopy in the attaching map. We write these data before comparing them with geometric duality. The boundary comparison below proves agreement of the localization and continuous-inertia pairings from the specified ordinary operations, including the Kummer divisor sign. An isomorphism between the underlying objects alone would not prove that agreement.

Use a finite extension \(E/\mathbf Q_\ell\). For the structure map \(a_X:X\to S\), put \(\omega_X^\delta=a_X^!E(1)[2]\), and write \(D_X^\delta\) for its duality. Write \(D_Z\) for duality on \(Z=X_s\), with its field-relative dualizing complex \(\omega_Z\). The ordinary purity and restriction comparisons required here are

\[ i^*D_X^\delta K\simeq D_Zi^!K, \qquad j^*D_X^\delta K\simeq D_{X_\eta}(j^*K)(1)[2]. \tag{E.1} \]

Proposition B.1d proves these evaluation-defined exchanges and family biduality from the specified ambient operations, B.1b, B.1c and the generic nearby/boundary-trace comparisons. The ambient construction and its ordinary and normalized adic providers remain exact prerequisites, not an assumed family-biduality theorem. For a trait coming from a smooth curve, this is the absolute total-space normalization. The ordinary torsion stage is supplied by Proposition B.1e; its enhanced, completed and rational comparisons remain distinct obligations.

Proposition E.1 (full-inertia comparison under the stated foundational inputs). At the arbitrary henselian-trait scope of Appendix D, the required comparison is

\[ D_Z\Phi_fK\simeq\tau\Phi_f(D_X^\delta K)(-1). \tag{E.2} \]

The deduction below proves this from Appendix D, (E.1), functorial localization and tensor adjunctions, multiplicative continuous descent, and divisor-oriented purity. It includes the boundary-pairing comparison and compatibility with specialization and variation. Complete proofs of the ordinary and normalized adic foundations are still required, so the proposition remains conditional on those inputs. Its assigned scope has not been reduced to a point or to tame inertia.

Separate the forced summand by its actual map

Set \(A=i^*K\), \(C=R\psi j^*K\), and \(B=R\Gamma(I,C)\). Descent identifies the attaching map with \(a:A\to B\), and localization identifies \(i^!K=\operatorname{Fib}(a)\). All fibres and cones below retain the homotopies in this map.

The averaging projector of Appendix B and the bounded Fitting construction of Section 5 split \(C=C_u\oplus C_r\). Here \(C_u\) is the generalized eigenvalue-one part of the \(H\)-invariants; \(C_r\) includes both the other tame eigenvalues and the entire complement of the \(H\)-invariants. This is a functorial split. Changing the tame generator to a unit power preserves its eigenvalue-one part, as does arithmetic conjugation, so it preserves residue-field descent.

The intrinsic map of Appendix C restricts to an isomorphism \(\iota_r:C_r\to\tau^{-1}C_r\). On the nonunipotent \(H\)-invariant part its coordinate map is the invertible operator \(T-1\); on the complement of the \(H\)-invariants it is the identity. Thus its fibre is zero and \(R\Gamma(I,C_r)=0\). The inverse of \(\iota_r\) contracts the two-term complex, giving the nullhomotopy of the other specialization component. Consequently

\[ \Phi_fK\simeq\Phi_uK\oplus C_r[-1], \qquad \Phi_uK=\operatorname{Fib}(A\longrightarrow C_u). \tag{E.3} \]

The simplification of the positive twist on this summand is the specific natural isomorphism \(\tau(\iota_r):\tau C_r\to C_r\). On the nonunipotent tame part this is multiplication by \(T-1\), not a literal identity of its two arithmetic actions. This distinction also applies to the corresponding summand of the dual.

Compute the dual group complex with both signs

On \(C_u\), the finite series \(c(t)=\log(1+t)/t\), where \(t=T-1\), is invertible. The change of the second generator by \(c(t)\) converts the resolution of Appendix C to \(G(C_u)=[C_u\xrightarrow{\nu}C_u(-1)]\), in group degrees zero and one, where \(\nu=\log T\) includes the Tate line. The augmentation is still projection from group degree zero. The denominators in this step require the field \(E\).

Put \(V=D_ZC_u\) and \(m=D_Z\nu:V(1)\to V\). The contragredient action is \((T^{-1})^{\mathsf t}\), so its logarithm satisfies \(\nu_V(1)=-m\). Indeed, the finite logarithm commutes with transpose, and \(\log(T^{-1})=-\log T\); both follow by substituting the nilpotent operator into the formal power-series identities. The dual group complex and the shifted group complex therefore have the same two-term description:

\[ \begin{array}{c|cc|c} &\text{degree }-1&\text{degree }0&\text{differential}\\ D_ZG(C_u)&V(1)&V&m\\ G(V)(1)[1]&V(1)&V&-\nu_V(1)=m. \end{array} \]

The minus sign from shifting a cochain complex cancels the minus sign in the contragredient logarithm. Omitting either one changes the comparison. With the usual totalization for an internal complex, this gives

\[ D_ZR\Gamma(I,C_u)\simeq R\Gamma(I,D_ZC_u)(1)[1]. \tag{E.4} \]

Here is the pairing that fixes the signs, before any geometric identification. Pair the degree-zero term of \(G(C_u)\) with the degree-zero term of \(G(V)(1)[1]\) by evaluation; pair their degree-one and degree-minus-one terms by negative evaluation. On \(c\otimes v\) of total degree minus one, the differential followed by this pairing is \(-\langle\nu c,v\rangle+\langle c,mv\rangle=0\). These are precisely the dual evaluations on the two resolution terms. For complexes, the internal differentials obey the same rule with the Koszul signs from their degrees. Computing on resolutions for derived internal Hom and totalizing gives the displayed natural comparison. The ordinary constructible biduality and coefficient comparisons used to do this are still required foundations.

For trivial coefficients the resulting degree-one trace is \(H^1(I,E(1))\to E\): evaluate the continuous homomorphism on the chosen generator and contract with its Tate basis. A generator change multiplies that value and the dual basis by inverse factors, so this trace is intrinsic. The geometric identification below uses this normalization together with the negative localization boundary in the fibre-coordinate identification (E.8).

Keep the attaching homotopy in the cancellation

We use the following explicit cochain conventions:

\[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Cof}(f)^n&=Y^n\oplus X^{n+1},& d(y,x)&=(d_Yy+fx,-d_Xx),\\ \operatorname{Fib}(f)^n&=X^n\oplus Y^{n-1},& d(x,y)&=(d_Xx,fx-d_Yy) \end{aligned} \]

for \(f:X\to Y\). The second model maps to \(\operatorname{Cof}(f)[-1]\) by \((x,y)\mapsto(-y,x)\). A resolved model here represents the finite diagram and its specified homotopies in the ambient enhanced derived category; it does not mean a bounded resolution by constructible injective sheaves. In these coordinates the map \(a:A\to G(C_u)\) consists of specialization \(s:A\to C_u\) and a degree-minus-one map \(h:A\to C_u(-1)\), with \(\nu s=d h+h d\). The normalized variation is \((a_0,c)\mapsto h a_0-\nu c\) on \(\operatorname{Fib}(s)\). The canonical map from \(C_u[-1]\) sends \(c\) to \((0,-c)\), so their composite is \(\nu[-1]\), with the sign fixed by the logarithmic change of generator from Appendix C.

Now write \(W=D_ZA\), \(Q=D_ZB=\operatorname{Cof}(m:V(1)\to V)\), and \(b=D_Za:Q\to W\). Let \(g:V\to W\) be the restriction of \(b\), namely the dual specialization. In a resolved model, the other component is a degree-minus-one map \(k:V(1)\to W\). The chain-map equation for \(b\) is \(g m=d_W k+k d_{V(1)}\). It is the dual attaching homotopy, and cannot be discarded. Dualizing localization yields

\[ i^*D_X^\delta K\simeq U=\operatorname{Cof}(b:Q\to W). \tag{E.5} \]

Appendix D identifies the unipotent nearby object of the dual input with \(V(1)[2]\). The candidate for its geometric specialization is

\[ p:U\longrightarrow Q[1]\longrightarrow V(1)[2]. \tag{E.6} \]

The second arrow is the group augmentation under (E.4): \(Q[1]\) has differential \(-m=\nu_V(1)\). In coordinates,

\[ \begin{aligned} U^n&=W^n\oplus V^{n+1}\oplus V(1)^{n+2},\\ d_U(w,v,z)&=(d_Ww+gv+kz,-d_Vv-mz,d_{V(1)}z),\\ p(w,v,z)&=z. \end{aligned} \]

The equality \(d_U^2=0\) uses exactly the displayed homotopy equation. Its kernel is \(\operatorname{Cof}(g:V\to W)\), but a calculation of the fibre also records the actual contraction. A fibre element is \((w,v,z,y)\), where \(y\in V(1)^{n+1}\), and its differential is

\[ d(w,v,z,y)= (d_Ww+gv+kz,-d_Vv-mz,dz,z-dy). \]

Define the inclusion \(e(w,v)=(w,v,0,0)\), the retraction \(r(w,v,z,y)=(w-ky,v+my)\), and the degree-minus-one homotopy \(H(w,v,z,y)=(0,0,y,0)\). Direct substitution gives \(re=1\), \(rd=dr\), and \(dH+Hd=1-er\). For example, the first component of the latter identity is \(ky\), and the second is \(-my\); these are the terms lost by ignoring the attaching homotopy. Thus \(\operatorname{Fib}(p)\simeq\operatorname{Cof}(g)=D_Z\Phi_uK\). This is a calculation of maps of resolved complexes, not just an equality of their cohomology dimensions. It is natural for maps of attaching diagrams, with the homotopies transported along those maps.

The geometric boundary pairing

We now compare the two pairings with their actual boundary maps. The argument uses the ordinary functorial localization, tensor and exceptional adjunctions, open and proper base change, and multiplicative continuous descent. These are the same ambient operations used in Appendix D. Their geometric construction and normalized adic realization remain prerequisite obligations; the argument below proves the compatibility from these specified operations.

Write \(B_X(N)=i^*Rj_*N\) for an object on the generic fibre. Localization identifies it with \(G(R\psi_XN)\). Fix the isomorphism

\[ \lambda_N:B_X(N)[-1]\xrightarrow{\sim}i^!j_!N \tag{E.8} \]

by the fibre coordinates already used above: \(i^!j_!N=\operatorname{Fib}(0\to B_X(N))\), and \(\lambda_N(b)=(0,b)\). Thus \(\lambda_N\) is the negative of the boundary \(B_X(N)[-1]\to i^!j_!N\) in the rotated localization triangle. That boundary sends \(b\) to \((0,-b)\). Keeping this distinction is essential for the purity sign.

Localization and multiplication. For generic-fibre objects \(M,N\), let \(\mu:B_X(M)\otimes^L B_X(N)\to B_X(M\otimes^L N)\) be the cup product. Then the square

\[ \begin{array}{ccc} B_X(M)\otimes^L B_X(N)[-1]&\xrightarrow{\mu[-1]}&B_X(M\otimes^L N)[-1]\\ \downarrow{1\otimes\lambda_N}&&\downarrow{\lambda_{M\otimes N}}\\ i^*Rj_*M\otimes^L i^!j_!N&\longrightarrow&i^!j_!(M\otimes^L N) \end{array} \tag{E.9} \]

commutes. The top arrow includes the tensor-shift isomorphism: a homogeneous element of degree \(p\) in the first factor acquires \((-1)^p\) when the shift in the second factor is moved outside the tensor product.

Here is a proof that also specifies the lower arrow. Tensor the localization triangle for \(j_!N\) with \(Rj_*M\). The closed projection formula identifies its first term with \(i_*(B_X(M)\otimes^L i^!j_!N)\); the open projection formula identifies its middle term with \(j_!(M\otimes^L N)\). The adjoint of the tensor product of the two open-restriction counits supplies the map from its third term to \(Rj_*(M\otimes^L N)\). These three maps form a morphism to the localization triangle of \(j_!(M\otimes^L N)\). On applying \(i^*\), the middle terms vanish and the third map is \(\mu\). The induced map of fibres is therefore the shifted cup product. In fibre coordinates it is the square (E.9); replacing each fibre-coordinate identification by the triangle boundary inserts a minus sign in both vertical arrows and leaves the square unchanged. The tensor-shift sign follows directly by comparing \(d(x\otimes y)=dx\otimes y+(-1)^p x\otimes dy\) before and after shifting.

The descent identification preserves this cup product. The direct-image and invariant functors have products adjoint to the tensor products of their pullback counits; the intervening restrictions are exact symmetric monoidal functors. In a descent resolution, taking these adjoints successively gives the nearby-cycle product followed by the continuous group-cochain product. Taking the composite counits at once gives the product on \(i^*Rj_*\). The counit of a composite adjunction is the composite of its counits, so these constructions agree. This identifies the maps, rather than just the cohomology groups of a descent spectral sequence. It applies to the entire inertia action; no tame replacement is made here.

Transporting a boundary through a map. Let \(h:X\to Y\) be separated and of finite type over the trait. There is a specified map

\[ b_h:Rh_{s!}i_X^!j_{X!}N\longrightarrow i_Y^!j_{Y!}Rh_{\eta!}N. \]

It is the adjoint, under \(i_{Y*}\dashv i_Y^!\), of

\[ i_{Y*}Rh_{s!}i_X^!j_{X!}N \simeq Rh_!i_{X*}i_X^!j_{X!}N \longrightarrow Rh_!j_{X!}N \simeq j_{Y!}Rh_{\eta!}N. \]

The middle arrow is the closed-support counit. Under (E.8) and descent, this map is

\[ Rh_{s!}G_X(R\psi_XN)[-1] \xrightarrow{\kappa} G_Y(Rh_{s!}R\psi_XN)[-1] \xrightarrow{G_Y(\alpha_h)[-1]} G_Y(R\psi_YRh_{\eta!}N)[-1]. \tag{E.10} \]

Here \(\alpha_h\) is the map defined in Appendix D. The exchange map \(\kappa\) is the adjoint comparison with derived invariants, obtained from the base-change identity for pullback to the inertia topos. It is not being asserted to be an isomorphism for a general \(h\).

To prove (E.10), first let \(h=u\) be open. Transpose both proposed maps under \(u_{s!}\dashv u_s^*\). Open base change and \(u_\eta^*u_{\eta!}N=N\) identify their targets with \(i_X^!j_{X!}N\). The transpose of \(b_u\) is the identity, by the counit used to define it. The transpose of \(\alpha_u\) is also the identity by its definition. Open restriction preserves the localization fibre and \(\lambda\); hence the second transpose is that same identity, with the same fibre-coordinate sign. Adjunction proves equality.

For \(h=p\) proper, proper base change gives

\[ Rp_{s*}i_X^*Rj_{X*}N \simeq i_Y^*Rp_*Rj_{X*}N \simeq i_Y^*Rj_{Y*}Rp_{\eta*}N. \]

Apply the same base-change maps to the localization triangle. Its closed-support arrow is the adjoint defining \(b_p\), so its fibre map gives \(b_p\) under \(\lambda\). Applying geometric-generic restriction followed by descent gives the right side of (E.10), since \(\alpha_p\) is that proper base-change map. Thus both are obtained from the same morphism of localization triangles. Finally choose a compactification \(h=pu\). Both constructions compose: for the first this follows by composing the displayed closed-support counits; for the second it follows by composing the pullback adjunctions defining \(\kappa\) and the maps \(\alpha\). The counit identity \(\epsilon_{vu}=\epsilon_v\circ Rv_!\epsilon_u\) identifies these composites. This proves (E.10), and also its independence of the compactification, under the ordinary compactification and coherence inputs of Appendix D.

The base-trait trace and its sign. Put \(\Omega_S=E_S(1)[2]\). Let \(q_S\) be the map

\[ G(E(1)[2])[-1] \xrightarrow{\lambda}i_S^!j_{S!}E_\eta(1)[2] \longrightarrow i_S^!\Omega_S\simeq E_s. \tag{E.11} \]

The last identification is the divisor-oriented purity of Proposition B.1c, with its compatible finite, complete and rational maps. We check that \(q_S\) is the positive group trace, including the sign relating that divisor class to Kummer theory. The passage from this base trace to a general \(X/S\) still uses the separate family-level exceptional adjunction and duality inputs.

At level \(\mathbf Z/\ell^n\), choose a uniformizer \(\pi\). Its Kummer torsor defines a class \(\kappa_\pi\) on the generic point. On inertia it is the tame character \(I\to\mathbf Z_\ell(1)\) reduced modulo \(\ell^n\): compatible roots of \(\pi\) are taken to each other by their root-of-unity ratios. Its value on the selected tame generator is the selected Tate basis. The divisor class is formed in the other order: take the localization boundary of \(\pi\) in \(\mathbf G_m\), then the Kummer boundary with supports. These two boundary operations anticommute. To see the sign, resolve the Kummer sequence and the restriction-to-the-open map in two directions; in the total complex the second differential on column \(r\) is multiplied by \((-1)^r\). Moving once in each direction in the opposite order therefore changes the sign. Equivalently, the two successive lifts defining the connecting maps have opposite total differentials. Consequently

\[ \partial_{\mathrm{loc}}\kappa_\pi=-\operatorname{cl}_{\ell^n}(s). \tag{E.12} \]

This is the convention in the free author edition of SGA 4½, Cycle, 2.1.1–2.1.3, printed pp. 138–139. It also explains the negative fundamental-class description on Illusie's printed p. 37. The author's erratum changes the upper differential of the shifted diagram there to \(1-T\); it does not remove (E.12).

In the fibre convention of this appendix, the ordinary localization boundary sends \(b\) to \((0,-b)\). In contrast, (E.11) first uses \(\lambda(b)=(0,b)\). Thus (E.12) and the divisor orientation give \(q_S(\kappa_\pi)=1\). The group trace has the same value by its defining evaluation on the tame character. There is no further component of the map to determine: \(G(E(1))[1]\) has cohomology only in degrees \(-1,0\), with degree-zero cohomology \(E\); its negative truncation belongs to \(D^{\leq-1}\), so every map from that truncation to \(E\in D^{\geq0}\) vanishes. A morphism from \(G(E(1))[1]\) to \(E\) is therefore determined by the induced map from its degree-zero truncation. Both maps induce the identity. This also works with residue-field descent, without choosing a splitting of its Galois extension.
